title: Hypertension: Diagnosis and Management
content: Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is defined as a sustained clinic blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher. Most cases are primary (essential) hypertension with no identifiable secondary cause. Secondary causes include renal artery stenosis, chronic kidney disease, primary aldosteronism, and obstructive sleep apnea. Hypertension is usually asymptomatic, which is why it is called the silent killer; it damages the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes over years. Lifestyle modification is the foundation of management: dietary sodium below 2 grams per day, the DASH diet, regular aerobic exercise, weight loss, and limiting alcohol. Pharmacologic therapy is started when blood pressure remains above 140/90 despite lifestyle changes, or immediately when readings are above 160/100. First-line agents include ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) such as losartan, calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine, and thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone. Beta blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension. Patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease are usually started on an ACE inhibitor or ARB because of their renoprotective effects. Most patients need two or more agents from different classes to reach target blood pressure below 140/90, or below 130/80 in high-risk groups. Routine monitoring includes blood pressure at every visit, yearly renal function and electrolytes while on diuretics or ACE inhibitors, and cardiovascular risk assessment.

title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Overview and Treatment
content: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterised by insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction, resulting in chronic hyperglycaemia. Diagnosis is confirmed by a fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance value of 200 mg/dL or higher, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with symptoms. Classic symptoms include polyuria, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss. Management begins with lifestyle intervention: medical nutrition therapy, at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week, and weight loss of 5 to 10 percent. Metformin is the first-line pharmacologic agent for most patients, started at diagnosis alongside lifestyle change. If glycaemic targets are not met after three months, a second agent is added; common choices include sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, or basal insulin. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists are preferred in patients with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease because they reduce cardiovascular events. HbA1c is generally measured every three months until stable, then every six months. Targets are individualised; an HbA1c below 7 percent is a common goal for non-pregnant adults, but higher targets are acceptable in frail or older patients. Annual screening for complications includes diabetic retinopathy screening, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, foot examination, and lipid profile. Hypoglycaemia risk increases with insulin and sulfonylureas; patients should be counselled on recognition and treatment with fast-acting carbohydrates.

title: Metformin: Mechanism, Use, and Side Effects
content: Metformin is a biguanide and the first-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes mellitus. It lowers blood glucose primarily by reducing hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis) and improving peripheral insulin sensitivity. It does not cause hypoglycaemia when used alone, does not promote weight gain, and is associated with modest weight loss, which makes it attractive in overweight patients. It is available as immediate-release and extended-release tablets; extended release reduces gastrointestinal intolerance. The typical starting dose is 500 mg once or twice daily with meals, titrated gradually to a maximum of 2000 to 2550 mg per day in divided doses. The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal: nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort, and a metallic taste; these usually improve over time. A rare but serious adverse effect is lactic acidosis, which occurs almost exclusively in patients with renal impairment, severe liver disease, heart failure requiring treatment, sepsis, or during major surgery or iodinated contrast studies. Metformin should be held before and after procedures using iodinated contrast in patients at risk of acute kidney injury. It is contraindicated when the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is below 30 mL/min per 1.73 m2. Long-term use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, so periodic B12 monitoring is recommended, especially in patients with peripheral neuropathy. The tablet should be taken with food to minimise gastrointestinal side effects.

title: Insulin Therapy: Types and Principles
content: Insulin is a peptide hormone produced by pancreatic beta cells that enables glucose uptake into cells and suppresses hepatic glucose production. In type 1 diabetes, insulin therapy is essential because the pancreas produces little or no insulin. In type 2 diabetes, insulin is added when oral agents fail to achieve glycaemic targets, often after several years of disease, and it is also used temporarily during hospitalisation, surgery, or severe illness. Insulin preparations differ mainly by onset and duration of action. Rapid-acting insulins such as lispro and aspart act within 15 minutes and last 3 to 5 hours; they are given with meals. Short-acting regular insulin peaks at 30 to 60 minutes. Intermediate-acting NPH insulin lasts 10 to 16 hours. Long-acting basal insulins such as glargine and detemir provide a steady background insulin level over about 24 hours and are given once daily. Basal-bolus regimens combine a long-acting insulin once or twice daily with rapid-acting insulin before meals, mimicking normal physiology. Common adverse effects include hypoglycaemia, weight gain, and injection-site lipohypertrophy. Hypoglycaemia is the most important safety concern; symptoms include sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion, and in severe cases seizures or coma. Treatment of mild hypoglycaemia is 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, repeated after 15 minutes if symptoms persist. Severe hypoglycaemia with altered consciousness requires glucagon or intravenous dextrose. Insulin doses must be adjusted during intercurrent illness, when renal function changes, and around procedures.

title: Asthma: Diagnosis and Stepwise Management
content: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterised by variable airflow obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and respiratory symptoms that vary over time: wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough, often worse at night or in the early morning and triggered by allergens, exercise, cold air, or respiratory infections. Diagnosis is supported by spirometry showing reversible obstruction: an increase in FEV1 of at least 12 percent and 200 mL after bronchodilator. Management follows a stepwise approach. All patients need education, inhaler technique review, trigger avoidance, and a written action plan. Short-acting beta-agonists (SABAs) such as salbutamol are used for quick relief of symptoms. For patients using a SABA more than twice a week, a daily controller inhaler is added: inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) such as budesonide or fluticasone are the cornerstone of anti-inflammatory therapy. For persistent symptoms despite low-dose ICS, options include increasing ICS dose, adding a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) such as formoterol or salmeterol, or adding a leukotriene receptor antagonist such as montelukast. The preferred option in adults is ICS-formoterol as both maintenance and reliever therapy. Severe asthma may require high-dose ICS, LABA, long-acting muscarinic antagonists, biologics such as anti-IgE or anti-IL5 agents, and oral corticosteroids for exacerbations. Uncontrolled asthma is indicated by daytime symptoms more than twice a week, nocturnal awakenings, reliever use more than twice a week, or activity limitation. Exacerbations are treated with repeated inhaled bronchodilators and early oral corticosteroids; red flags include inability to speak full sentences, silent chest, and cyanosis.

title: Salbutamol (Albuterol): Reliever Bronchodilator
content: Salbutamol, known as albuterol in North America, is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist (SABA) used as a reliever in asthma and COPD. It acts within minutes by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle, providing rapid relief of wheeze, cough, and breathlessness. It is delivered by metered-dose inhaler, dry-powder inhaler, or nebuliser; the inhaled route maximises bronchodilation with fewer systemic effects. The usual dose is one to two puffs (100 to 200 micrograms) as needed for symptom relief, repeated after 20 minutes if needed. Onset of action is within 5 minutes and the effect lasts 3 to 6 hours. Common side effects are tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, and headache, reflecting beta-2 and mild beta-1 stimulation; they are dose-related and usually transient. Salbutamol is not a controller: using a reliever more than twice a week indicates poor asthma control and the need for an anti-inflammatory controller such as inhaled corticosteroids. In an acute asthma attack, up to 4 to 10 puffs via a spacer or nebulised salbutamol can be given, repeated every 20 minutes in the first hour while awaiting further care. Hypokalaemia is a rare but recognised effect, especially at high doses. Patients should be counselled that increasing reliever use is a warning sign of worsening control and should trigger a medical review.

title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
content: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a preventable and treatable lung disease characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and alveolar abnormalities, usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases, overwhelmingly tobacco smoke. Spirometry confirms the diagnosis when the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio is below 0.70. Symptoms include progressive dyspnoea, chronic cough, and sputum production. Smoking cessation is the single most effective intervention and slows disease progression. Pharmacologic therapy is bronchodilator-based: long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) such as tiotropium and long-acting beta-agonists (LABAs) such as salmeterol or indacaterol improve symptoms, exercise tolerance, and quality of life, and reduce exacerbations. Combination LAMA-LABA therapy is recommended for patients with persistent symptoms or frequent exacerbations. Inhaled corticosteroids are added in patients with a history of repeated exacerbations and elevated blood eosinophils. Pulmonary rehabilitation, annual influenza vaccination, and pneumococcal vaccination are core components of care. Long-term oxygen therapy is indicated in chronic severe hypoxaemia, defined as resting PaO2 of 55 mmHg or lower, or 56 to 59 mmHg with evidence of cor pulmonale; it is used at least 15 hours per day. Acute exacerbations are characterised by worsening dyspnoea and increased sputum volume or purulence; treatment includes short-acting bronchodilators, oral corticosteroids for 5 days, and antibiotics when sputum is purulent or pneumonia is suspected. Non-invasive ventilation reduces the need for intubation in hypercapnic respiratory failure.

title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
content: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is an acute infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside of healthcare settings. Common pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and respiratory viruses. Typical symptoms are fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and malaise; examination may reveal crackles and bronchial breathing. Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by chest imaging, usually a chest radiograph showing a new infiltrate. Severity is assessed with tools such as CURB-65, which scores confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate of 30 or more, low blood pressure, and age 65 or older; higher scores warrant hospital admission. Outpatient treatment for previously healthy adults without comorbidities is usually amoxicillin or doxycycline for 5 days. In patients with comorbidities or in regions with high macrolide resistance, amoxicillin-clavulanate plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin, is used. Hospitalised patients receive a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone. Severely ill patients require intensive care, oxygen, and broad-spectrum cover. Complications include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, and sepsis. Vaccination with pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and annual influenza vaccine reduces the risk of CAP in at-risk adults. Follow-up imaging is reserved for patients at risk of malignancy, such as smokers over 50, or those with slow resolution.

title: Tuberculosis: Clinical Features and Treatment
content: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus transmitted by airborne droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Primary infection is often asymptomatic and contained by the immune system; latent TB infection has a positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay with no active disease. Active pulmonary TB classically presents with a cough lasting more than three weeks, haemoptysis, night sweats, fever, weight loss, and anorexia. Chest radiograph typically shows upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or hilar lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is confirmed by sputum smear microscopy, nucleic acid amplification tests such as GeneXpert MTB/RIF, and mycobacterial culture. Standard treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is a 6-month regimen: a 2-month intensive phase with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by a 4-month continuation phase with isoniazid and rifampicin. Directly observed therapy improves adherence. Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer that interacts with many drugs, including warfarin, oral contraceptives, and antiretrovirals. Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy, prevented with pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Patients should be monitored for hepatotoxicity, with liver enzymes checked at baseline and if symptoms develop. Multidrug-resistant TB requires longer regimens with second-line agents and specialist care. All household contacts should be screened, and latent TB is treated with regimens such as 4 months of daily rifampicin or 3 months of weekly isoniazid-rifapentine.

title: Urinary Tract Infection: Cystitis and Pyelonephritis
content: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection of the urinary system. Cystitis, infection of the bladder, presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort; fever is usually absent. Pyelonephritis, infection of the kidney, presents with flank pain, fever, rigors, nausea, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Escherichia coli causes 75 to 90 percent of uncomplicated UTIs. Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women is typically diagnosed clinically; a urine dipstick showing nitrites or leukocyte esterase supports the diagnosis, and a midstream urine culture is reserved for recurrent, complicated, or failed cases. First-line treatment for uncomplicated cystitis is a short course of nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days where resistance is low. Fosfomycin is a single-dose alternative. Pregnancy changes management: nitrofurantoin is safe in most trimesters, but any bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated because of risks to the fetus. Pyelonephritis requires 7 to 14 days of antibiotics, often starting with a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin, or an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin for initial therapy in sicker patients. Complicated UTIs occur in patients with catheters, obstruction, structural abnormalities, immunosuppression, or male sex. Recurrent cystitis can be reduced with behavioural measures, and in select cases with postcoital prophylaxis, continuous low-dose prophylaxis, or vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal women.

title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
content: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) occurs when gastric contents reflux into the oesophagus, causing troublesome symptoms or complications. Typical symptoms are heartburn (retrosternal burning) and regurgitation, often after meals or when lying down. Atypical symptoms include chronic cough, hoarseness, sore throat, and non-cardiac chest pain. Alarm features that warrant prompt endoscopy include dysphagia, odynophagia, unintentional weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding, vomiting, and iron-deficiency anaemia. Lifestyle measures help: weight loss, avoiding meals within 3 hours of bedtime, elevating the head of the bed, and reducing alcohol, tobacco, and large fatty meals. Acid suppression is the mainstay of pharmacotherapy. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, and pantoprazole are the most effective agents and are used once daily 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast for 4 to 8 weeks in erosive disease. Histamine-2 receptor antagonists such as famotidine are an alternative, particularly for nocturnal symptoms or on-demand relief. Antacids and alginates provide rapid short-term symptom relief. Long-term PPI use should be at the lowest effective dose, because prolonged use is associated with risks including hypomagnesaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, increased fracture risk, and Clostridioides difficile infection. Surgical fundoplication is reserved for patients with confirmed reflux who are refractory to medical therapy or who prefer surgery; it is also considered in large hiatus hernias. Barrett's oesophagus, a metaplastic change found at endoscopy, requires surveillance because of the small risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

title: Proton Pump Inhibitors: Omeprazole and Class Effects
content: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are the most potent acid-suppressing drugs available. Omeprazole is the prototype; esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, and rabeprazole are related agents. PPIs irreversibly inhibit the hydrogen-potassium ATPase pump on gastric parietal cells, the final common pathway of gastric acid secretion, so they suppress both basal and stimulated acid. They are indicated for gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive oesophagitis, peptic ulcer disease, Helicobacter pylori eradication (combined with antibiotics), prevention of NSAID-induced ulcers in high-risk patients, and pathological hypersecretory states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Optimal timing is 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal of the day; the drug needs to be taken on a regular schedule rather than on demand for maximal effect in erosive disease. Common adverse effects include headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and nausea. Long-term use is associated with hypomagnesaemia, reduced absorption of vitamin B12 and calcium, a modest increase in hip fracture risk, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, and increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. Acid rebound can occur when a PPI is stopped abruptly. PPIs interact with clopidogrel by competing for CYP2C19, potentially reducing its antiplatelet effect; pantoprazole is less affected. Omeprazole is metabolised by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 and can raise levels of diazepam, phenytoin, and warfarin. The general principle is to use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed.

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Helicobacter pylori
content: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) refers to mucosal breaks in the stomach or duodenum. The two dominant causes are Helicobacter pylori infection and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs); less common causes include Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and smoking. Duodenal ulcers classically cause epigastric pain that improves with food and recurs 2 to 3 hours after meals or at night; gastric ulcers cause pain that worsens with eating. Alarm features include haematemesis, melaena, anaemia, weight loss, and persistent vomiting. Diagnosis is by upper endoscopy; H. pylori can be diagnosed by urea breath test, stool antigen test, or endoscopic biopsy with rapid urease test. Testing for H. pylori should be performed before initiating long-term PPI therapy, because PPIs suppress the organism and cause false-negative results. Eradication therapy is a 14-day regimen of a PPI plus two antibiotics, for example clarithromycin and amoxicillin (triple therapy), with bismuth quadruple therapy as an alternative where clarithromycin resistance is high. Successful eradication is confirmed at least 4 weeks after completing antibiotics and 2 weeks after stopping the PPI, using a urea breath test or stool antigen test. NSAID-associated ulcers are managed by stopping the NSAID where possible, adding a PPI, and treating H. pylori if present. Patients who must continue aspirin or NSAIDs for cardiovascular protection receive co-therapy with a PPI. Complications of peptic ulcers include bleeding, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction; bleeding ulcers are treated endoscopically with injection, thermal coagulation, or clips.

title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome
content: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a disorder of gut-brain interaction characterised by recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation, associated with a change in stool frequency or form. It is diagnosed using Rome IV criteria: abdominal pain at least one day per week in the last three months, associated with two or more of pain related to defecation, change in stool frequency, or change in stool form. IBS is subclassified as IBS-C (constipation predominant), IBS-D (diarrhoea predominant), IBS-M (mixed), or IBS-U (unclassified). It is a diagnosis made after excluding alarm features: unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, fever, family history of inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer, and onset after age 50. Limited investigations include full blood count, CRP or faecal calprotectin, coeliac serology, and thyroid function. Management is individualised. First-line advice covers diet and lifestyle: regular meals, adequate fluids, and limiting gas-producing foods; a trial of a low-FODMAP diet under dietitian supervision helps a subset of patients. Fibre supplements such as psyllium help IBS-C but insoluble bran may worsen symptoms. Pharmacologic options include antispasmodics such as hyoscine for pain, loperamide for diarrhoea, and osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol for constipation. Second-line agents include linaclotide, lubiprostone, and plecanatide for IBS-C, rifaximin and eluxadoline for IBS-D, and tricyclic antidepressants or SSRIs for global symptom control. Psychological therapies, including cognitive behavioural therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy, are effective for moderate to severe symptoms.

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Crohn's and Ulcerative Colitis
content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) comprises two chronic relapsing conditions: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (UC). Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus, with skip lesions and transmural inflammation; it commonly involves the terminal ileum and colon. Ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and rectum, with continuous mucosal inflammation starting at the rectum. Both typically present in young adults with diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Bloody diarrhoea is more typical of UC; perianal fistulas and abscesses suggest Crohn's disease. Diagnosis is made with colonoscopy and biopsy; faecal calprotectin is a useful non-invasive marker of mucosal inflammation. Extraintestinal manifestations include peripheral arthritis, sacroiliitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Treatment is stepped. Mild to moderate UC is treated with topical or oral 5-aminosalicylates such as mesalazine. Moderate Crohn's disease often responds to budesonide or systemic corticosteroids for induction, with azathioprine, methotrexate, or anti-TNF agents such as infliximab or adalimumab for maintenance. Anti-TNF therapy, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, and JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib are used in moderate to severe disease. Corticosteroids are for short-term induction only, not maintenance. Patients with colonic IBD require colonoscopic surveillance after 8 to 10 years because of increased colorectal cancer risk. Smoking worsens Crohn's disease and should be strongly discouraged; it is comparatively protective in ulcerative colitis, though not recommended.

title: Coeliac Disease
content: Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated systemic disorder triggered by dietary gluten, the storage protein in wheat, barley, and rye, in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. Gluten exposure causes small intestinal villous atrophy, leading to malabsorption. Classic presentations include chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, bloating, abdominal pain, and weight loss; iron-deficiency anaemia and fatigue are common in adults, and children may present with failure to thrive. Atypical presentations include dermatitis herpetiformis, an intensely itchy vesicular rash on the elbows and knees, osteoporosis, unexplained infertility, ataxia, and transaminitis. Diagnosis in adults relies on positive serology, IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody, followed by duodenal biopsy showing intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, and villous atrophy. Serologic testing requires a gluten-containing diet; at least 3 to 4 slices of bread daily for 6 weeks is the usual advice before testing. The only effective treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet. Response is monitored by symptom resolution and normalisation of serology and nutritional deficiencies; repeat biopsy is reserved for non-responders. Nutritional deficiencies of iron, folate, vitamin B12, calcium, and vitamin D should be corrected. Patients with coeliac disease have a slightly increased risk of intestinal lymphoma, particularly enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, and of other autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease. Annual follow-up is recommended to assess adherence and screen for complications.

title: Hepatitis B: Natural History and Management
content: Hepatitis B is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), a DNA virus transmitted by blood, sexual contact, and from mother to child. Acute infection may be asymptomatic or cause jaundice, fatigue, and raised transaminases; most immunocompetent adults clear the virus spontaneously, but infection acquired perinatally or in early childhood frequently becomes chronic. Chronic hepatitis B is defined by persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for more than 6 months. Serologic interpretation is important: HBsAg indicates infection; anti-HBs indicates immunity from vaccination or recovery; anti-HBc indicates past or ongoing infection. HBeAg-positive disease is associated with high viral replication and infectivity. Complications of chronic infection include cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma, so surveillance with six-monthly ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein is recommended. Treatment is indicated for patients with significant viral replication (HBV DNA above 2000 IU/mL) plus elevated ALT or moderate fibrosis, and for all patients with cirrhosis regardless of ALT. First-line oral agents are the nucleos(t)ide analogues tenofovir and entecavir, which are potent, well tolerated, and have a high barrier to resistance. Pegylated interferon is an alternative finite-duration therapy. Treatment is usually long-term and aims to suppress HBV DNA, normalise ALT, and reduce progression to cirrhosis and liver cancer. All household contacts and sexual partners should be tested, and vaccination with the three-dose hepatitis B vaccine is recommended for all unvaccinated individuals, including infants at birth. Antiviral prophylaxis is given to pregnant women with high viral load in the third trimester to reduce vertical transmission.

title: Hepatitis C: Diagnosis and Cure
content: Hepatitis C is caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV), an RNA virus transmitted primarily through blood, historically via contaminated transfusions and injecting drug use. Acute infection is usually asymptomatic; around 50 to 80 percent of infected people develop chronic infection. Chronic hepatitis C progresses slowly, and many patients are diagnosed incidentally years later through abnormal liver enzymes or screening. Complications include cirrhosis, decompensated liver disease, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis begins with anti-HCV antibody testing; a positive antibody test must be confirmed by HCV RNA, which distinguishes current infection from resolved infection. The advent of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy has transformed the disease: pangenotypic regimens such as sofosbuvir-velpatasvir, with or without voxilaprevir, achieve cure rates above 95 percent, including in patients with compensated cirrhosis. Treatment duration is usually 8 to 12 weeks, is oral, and is well tolerated with few side effects. A sustained virologic response (undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after completing therapy) is considered a cure. Patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis require ongoing surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma even after cure, typically six-monthly ultrasound. Vaccination against hepatitis A and B is recommended, and alcohol should be minimised. All patients should be screened at least once, and annual screening is recommended for people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men on pre-exposure prophylaxis, and others at ongoing risk. Direct-acting antivirals have important interactions, particularly with some antiretrovirals, amiodarone, and certain statins.

title: Cirrhosis and Its Complications
content: Cirrhosis is the end stage of chronic liver injury, characterised by diffuse fibrosis and regenerative nodules that distort hepatic architecture and impair function. Common causes are alcohol-related liver disease, chronic hepatitis B and C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly NAFLD), autoimmune hepatitis, and haemochromatosis. Cirrhosis is compensated when the liver still functions adequately and decompensated when complications appear: ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, or jaundice. Ascites is treated with dietary sodium restriction and spironolactone, often with furosemide; refractory ascites may require large-volume paracentesis or a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS). Oesophageal varices are screened by endoscopy at diagnosis and at intervals; non-selective beta blockers such as carvedilol or propranolol, or endoscopic band ligation, are used for primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding, and the combination for secondary prophylaxis. Acute variceal bleeding is managed with resuscitation, vasoactive drugs such as terlipressin, antibiotics, and urgent endoscopy with band ligation. Hepatic encephalopathy presents with a spectrum from subtle confusion and sleep disturbance to coma; it is treated with lactulose, and rifaximin is added for recurrent episodes. Patients with cirrhosis should avoid NSAIDs and alcohol, be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B, influenza, and pneumococcus, and undergo surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma with six-monthly ultrasound. The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score predicts mortality and guides transplant listing. Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for decompensated cirrhosis and early hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Chronic Kidney Disease: Staging and Management
content: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined by abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for more than 3 months, including a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m2 or markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria, haematuria, or structural abnormalities. The leading causes are diabetes mellitus and hypertension. CKD is staged G1 to G5 by GFR and A1 to A3 by albuminuria; the albumin-to-creatinine ratio is a stronger predictor of progression than GFR alone. Many patients are asymptomatic until advanced stages; fatigue, nocturia, and ankle swelling are late features. Management aims to slow progression and reduce cardiovascular risk. Blood pressure is targeted below 130/80 mmHg; ACE inhibitors or ARBs are first-line, particularly with albuminuria, and should be titrated to the maximum tolerated dose. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors such as dapagliflozin slow CKD progression and reduce heart failure and cardiovascular events in patients with albuminuria, including those without diabetes. Glycaemic control is important in diabetic kidney disease. Finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, is an option in diabetic CKD with albuminuria. Cardiovascular risk is addressed with statins and smoking cessation. Nephrotoxins to avoid include NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, and iodinated contrast where alternatives exist. Anaemia of CKD is managed with iron replacement and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents; renal bone disease with vitamin D and phosphate binders. Patients with eGFR below 30 should be referred to nephrology; preparation for kidney replacement therapy, including dialysis or transplantation, begins when eGFR falls below 20 to 25.

title: Heart Failure: Classification and Treatment
content: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, or requires elevated filling pressures to do so. It is classified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, LVEF 40 percent or less), mildly reduced (41-49 percent), and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF, 50 percent or more). Common causes include ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, valvular disease, and cardiomyopathy. Typical symptoms are breathlessness on exertion, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, and ankle swelling; signs include elevated jugular venous pressure, lung crackles, and peripheral oedema. Diagnosis is supported by natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) and echocardiography. Guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF is the four pillars: an ACE inhibitor or ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan), a beta blocker such as bisoprolol or carvedilol, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone, and an SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin; each class reduces mortality and hospitalisation. Loop diuretics such as furosemide relieve congestion. Patients with a left bundle branch block and LVEF of 35 percent or less on optimal therapy may benefit from cardiac resynchronisation therapy, and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is indicated for those at high risk of sudden death. HFpEF management focuses on congestion control, blood pressure treatment, and SGLT2 inhibitors, which modestly reduce hospitalisations. Lifestyle measures include sodium restriction, daily weighing to detect fluid gain, and exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation. Acute decompensation presents with severe breathlessness and fluid overload, requiring oxygen, intravenous diuretics, and sometimes inotropes or mechanical support.

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Rate, Rhythm, and Anticoagulation
content: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia, characterised by disorganised atrial activity and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. It is classified as paroxysmal (terminating within 7 days), persistent (lasting more than 7 days), and permanent. Risk factors include hypertension, age, heart failure, valvular disease, obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea, hyperthyroidism, and alcohol. Symptoms include palpitations, fatigue, dyspnoea, dizziness, and sometimes chest pain, though many patients are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally. AF increases the risk of ischaemic stroke about fivefold, because blood pools in the left atrial appendage and forms thrombi. Stroke risk is estimated with the CHA2DS2-VASc score, which awards points for congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke or transient ischaemic attack, vascular disease, and female sex; anticoagulation is recommended for men with a score of 2 or more and women with a score of 3 or more. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban and rivaroxaban are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF because of lower intracranial bleeding risk and no need for routine monitoring. Management also involves controlling the ventricular rate with beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem, or digoxin; target resting heart rate is below 110 beats per minute. Rhythm control with cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs such as amiodarone or flecainide, or catheter ablation is considered for symptomatic patients. Catheter ablation is superior to drug therapy for maintaining sinus rhythm in selected patients with paroxysmal AF. Lifestyle interventions, including weight loss and alcohol reduction, improve AF burden.

title: Warfarin: Anticoagulation and INR Monitoring
content: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, mechanical heart valves, and other thromboembolic conditions. It inhibits the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing the hepatic synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, and of proteins C and S. The therapeutic effect is monitored with the international normalised ratio (INR); the usual target is 2.0 to 3.0 for most indications, and 2.5 to 3.5 for mechanical mitral valves. Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic window and a slow onset: therapeutic anticoagulation takes several days, so overlap with a rapid-acting agent such as a low-molecular-weight heparin is required when treating acute thrombosis. The starting dose is typically 5 mg daily, adjusted according to INR. The INR must be checked frequently at initiation, then typically every 4 weeks once stable; point-of-care testing and dose-adjustment algorithms improve time in therapeutic range. Warfarin has many food and drug interactions. Foods rich in vitamin K, such as green leafy vegetables (kale, spinach, broccoli), can lower the INR, so intake should remain consistent rather than avoided. Major drug interactions include antibiotics, amiodarone, fluconazole, and rifampicin, which induce or inhibit CYP2C9. Bleeding is the main risk; major bleeding is treated with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma. Reversal of an elevated INR without bleeding depends on the level: for INR above 8 with minor bleeding, hold warfarin and give vitamin K; for supratherapeutic INR without bleeding, dose reduction or omission plus vitamin K may suffice. Warfarin is teratogenic and is avoided in pregnancy, where low-molecular-weight heparin is used instead.

title: Acute Myocardial Infarction (Heart Attack)
content: Acute myocardial infarction (MI) occurs when coronary blood flow is abruptly reduced, typically by rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed thrombosis, causing myocardial necrosis. The classic presentation is crushing central chest pain or pressure lasting more than 20 minutes, radiating to the left arm or jaw, associated with sweating, nausea, and breathlessness; atypical presentations, especially in women, the elderly, and diabetics, include epigastric pain, fatigue, and dyspnoea without chest pain. Diagnosis requires elevated cardiac troponin with a rising or falling pattern plus clinical evidence of myocardial ischaemia, ECG changes, or imaging. ST-elevation MI (STEMI) is a medical emergency requiring immediate reperfusion: primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 90 minutes of first medical contact where available, or fibrinolysis within 30 minutes when PCI is not available. Non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI) is managed with antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, and early invasive angiography in high-risk patients. Initial medical therapy includes aspirin 300 mg chewed immediately, a P2Y12 inhibitor such as ticagrelor or clopidogrel, an anticoagulant such as heparin, a beta blocker, a high-intensity statin such as atorvastatin 80 mg, and oxygen only if hypoxic. Long-term secondary prevention after MI is dual antiplatelet therapy for up to 12 months, lifelong low-dose aspirin in some regimens, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor, beta blocker, and cardiac rehabilitation. Complications include cardiogenic shock, acute pulmonary oedema, arrhythmias including ventricular fibrillation, and mechanical complications such as papillary muscle rupture. All patients should be counselled on smoking cessation and a heart-healthy diet.

title: Stroke and Transient Ischaemic Attack
content: Stroke is an acute neurological deficit caused by focal cerebral ischaemia (87 percent) or haemorrhage (13 percent). Transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain ischaemia without infarction, typically resolving within minutes to an hour. The FAST mnemonic captures the cardinal signs: facial droop, arm weakness, and speech disturbance, with time being critical. Acute ischaemic stroke is treated with intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients, and endovascular thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion within 6 to 24 hours in selected patients. Blood pressure is managed cautiously in the acute phase. Stroke mimics include hypoglycaemia, seizure, migraine with aura, and functional disorders. After the acute phase, secondary prevention is tailored to the mechanism. For cardioembolic stroke, typically from atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation with a DOAC or warfarin is started, usually within 1 to 2 weeks for moderate to large infarcts. For atherothrombotic stroke, treatment is dual antiplatelet therapy for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet therapy, a high-intensity statin, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation. Carotid endarterectomy is considered for symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50 to 99 percent. TIA is a warning sign: the risk of stroke in the 90 days after a TIA is up to 17 percent, highest in the first week, so patients are evaluated urgently with brain imaging, carotid imaging, and ECG, and started on antiplatelet therapy, a statin, and blood pressure management. Rehabilitation, including physiotherapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy, is the cornerstone of recovery.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis and Venous Thromboembolism
content: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is clot formation in the deep veins, most often of the lower limb. It commonly presents with unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and redness; the classic risk factors are captured by Virchow's triad: venous stasis (immobility, long travel, surgery), hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, oestrogen, thrombophilia), and endothelial injury (trauma, surgery, central lines). Proximal DVT (popliteal or above) carries a substantial risk of pulmonary embolism (PE), whereas distal calf DVT has a lower risk. Diagnosis uses a clinical prediction score such as the Wells score; a low-probability score with a negative D-dimer (an age-adjusted threshold is used in patients over 50) excludes DVT without imaging. Otherwise, compression ultrasonography confirms the diagnosis. Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of treatment: direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban or rivaroxaban are first-line for most patients, without requiring initial heparin. Warfarin requires heparin overlap until the INR reaches 2.0. Treatment duration is at least 3 months; extended anticoagulation is considered for unprovoked DVT, recurrent events, or persistent risk factors such as active cancer, where low-molecular-weight heparin or DOACs are preferred. Compression stockings reduce post-thrombotic syndrome, and early ambulation is encouraged. PE presents with sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, and tachycardia; massive PE with shock requires systemic thrombolysis. Preventive measures in hospitalised patients include pharmacological prophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin and mechanical devices such as intermittent pneumatic compression.

title: Iron Deficiency Anaemia
content: Iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia worldwide. Iron is required for haemoglobin synthesis, and deficiency leads to microcytic, hypochromic anaemia. Causes include chronic blood loss, most importantly from the gastrointestinal tract (peptic ulcers, colorectal cancer, angiodysplasia) and the menstrual tract in women, inadequate dietary intake, malabsorption such as in coeliac disease or after gastric surgery, and increased demand in pregnancy and infancy. Symptoms of anaemia are fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, and headache; severe deficiency causes pica (craving ice or soil), koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), and glossitis. Laboratory findings are low haemoglobin, low mean corpuscular volume (MCV), low serum ferritin, and low transferrin saturation. Serum ferritin is the best single test; a ferritin below 30 micrograms per litre confirms iron deficiency, although ferritin can be falsely normal or elevated in inflammation. Iron studies, including ferritin and transferrin saturation, help in ambiguous cases. Treatment is oral iron, typically ferrous sulfate 100 to 200 mg elemental iron on alternate days or daily, which improves absorption and reduces gastrointestinal side effects such as constipation and dark stools. Haemoglobin should rise by about 1 to 2 g/dL per month; iron is continued for 3 months after normalisation to replenish stores. Intravenous iron is used for intolerance, malabsorption, severe disease, or ongoing losses. The underlying cause must always be investigated: in men and postmenopausal women with iron deficiency, bidirectional endoscopy of the gastrointestinal tract is standard, with faecal immunochemical testing as an alternative first step in lower-risk patients.

title: Vitamin B12 Deficiency Anaemia
content: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neurological disease. B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum after binding to intrinsic factor produced by gastric parietal cells. Causes include pernicious anaemia, an autoimmune condition in which antibodies destroy parietal cells or neutralise intrinsic factor, gastric or ileal resection, Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum, long-term metformin use, and a strict vegan diet. Nitrous oxide exposure and proton pump inhibitors are less common causes. The anaemia is macrocytic, with an elevated MCV, and the peripheral smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Megaloblastic changes also affect the bone marrow and can cause pancytopenia. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise early and are sensitive markers when B12 levels are borderline. Neurological manifestations include symmetrical peripheral neuropathy with numbness and tingling, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts) presenting with ataxia and loss of vibration and proprioception, and cognitive impairment. Importantly, neurological damage can occur without anaemia, and if untreated for long, it may be irreversible. Treatment is replacement with hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin; initial intramuscular loading doses are given on alternate days for 2 weeks, followed by maintenance injections every 2 to 3 months, or high-dose oral B12 (1000 micrograms daily) for patients with normal absorption. Potassium levels should be monitored during the first days of treatment because red cell production can cause hypokalaemia. Response is monitored by reticulocytosis within a week, rising haemoglobin, and resolution of neurological symptoms. Pernicious anaemia requires lifelong replacement and is associated with an increased risk of gastric cancer, so endoscopy is considered.

title: Hypothyroidism
content: Hypothyroidism is the clinical state of deficient thyroid hormone action. Primary hypothyroidism, due to thyroid gland failure, accounts for over 99 percent of cases; the most common cause worldwide is iodine deficiency, while in iodine-sufficient regions autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's disease) predominates. Other causes include thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine therapy for Graves' disease, and certain drugs such as lithium and amiodarone. Symptoms develop insidiously: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, depression, menorrhagia, and bradycardia; physical signs include a slow relaxation phase of the ankle reflexes, periorbital oedema, and a goitre in Hashimoto's. Diagnosis is confirmed by a raised thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) with a low free thyroxine (T4); subclinical hypothyroidism shows a raised TSH with a normal free T4. Treatment is levothyroxine (synthetic T4), usually starting at 1.6 micrograms per kilogram daily, with lower starting doses and slower titration in the elderly and in patients with ischaemic heart disease to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmia. TSH is rechecked 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, with the goal of restoring TSH to the normal range. Once stable, TSH is monitored annually. Overtreatment causes symptoms of hyperthyroidism and increases the risk of atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis. In pregnancy, levothyroxine requirements increase by 30 to 50 percent, and thyroid function should be checked as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Myxoedema coma is a rare life-threatening decompensation with hypothermia, reduced consciousness, and hyponatraemia, treated in intensive care with intravenous levothyroxine and supportive measures.

title: Levothyroxine: Replacement Therapy
content: Levothyroxine is synthetic thyroxine (T4) used as replacement therapy for hypothyroidism and as suppressive therapy in thyroid cancer. It is a prohormone: the liver and other tissues convert T4 to the active hormone triiodothyronine (T3). The typical replacement dose is 1.6 micrograms per kilogram of body weight daily, though the starting dose is lower in the elderly and in patients with coronary artery disease, where therapy begins at 25 to 50 micrograms daily and is titrated slowly. Levothyroxine should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, ideally at the same time each day, because food, coffee, calcium, iron, and magnesium supplements reduce its absorption. It has a long half-life of about 7 days, so a steady state is reached 6 weeks after any dose change; TSH is measured 6 to 8 weeks after starting or adjusting the dose. The goal of therapy is a TSH in the normal reference range, except in thyroid cancer, where TSH is suppressed below 0.1 mIU/L to reduce stimulation of residual thyroid tissue. Overtreatment causes iatrogenic hyperthyroidism with palpitations, tremor, anxiety, and risks of atrial fibrillation and bone loss; undertreatment leaves symptoms of hypothyroidism. Significant drug interactions include cholestyramine and iron or calcium salts, which impair absorption, and phenytoin, rifampicin, and carbamazepine, which increase T4 metabolism. In pregnancy, the dose often needs to be increased by 30 to 50 percent, with monitoring every 4 to 6 weeks. Levothyroxine is among the most commonly prescribed medications worldwide, and adherence problems are the most frequent cause of an unexpectedly raised TSH.

title: Hyperthyroidism and Graves' Disease
content: Hyperthyroidism is the state of excess thyroid hormone, and thyrotoxicosis is the clinical syndrome that results. The most common cause is Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition in which thyroid-stimulating antibodies activate the TSH receptor, causing a diffuse goitre and excessive hormone production. Other causes include toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis (subacute, painless, postpartum) with hormone leak, and exogenous levothyroxine excess. Symptoms include weight loss despite increased appetite, palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, sweating, anxiety, diarrhoea, and oligomenorrhoea; signs include a goitre with a bruit, lid lag and lid retraction, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, and warm moist skin. Graves' disease may additionally cause orbitopathy, with proptosis, periorbital oedema, and diplopia, and rarely pretibial myxoedema. Diagnosis is by a suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and free T3, plus positive TSH-receptor antibodies in Graves' disease; thyroid scintigraphy helps differentiate causes when the picture is unclear. Treatment options are antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, and surgery. Carbimazole and methimazole (or propylthiouracil in the first trimester of pregnancy) are used for 12 to 18 months, with remission rates of about 50 percent; a serious adverse effect is agranulocytosis, so patients must be warned to stop the drug and seek urgent medical review if they develop a sore throat or fever. Beta blockers such as propranolol rapidly control adrenergic symptoms while definitive therapy takes effect. Radioactive iodine is effective and safe but causes permanent hypothyroidism in most patients, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy; it may worsen orbitopathy in smokers. Total thyroidectomy is an option for large goitres, suspected malignancy, or Graves' orbitopathy, and also causes permanent hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine.

title: Osteoporosis: Fracture Prevention
content: Osteoporosis is a skeletal disorder characterised by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk. It is most common in postmenopausal women because oestrogen deficiency accelerates bone resorption, but it also affects older men. Fractures of the hip, vertebrae, and wrist are characteristic; vertebral fractures may be silent or cause height loss and kyphosis, while hip fractures carry significant morbidity and mortality. Bone mineral density is measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at the hip and spine, reported as a T-score: a T-score of -2.5 or below defines osteoporosis, and between -1 and -2.5 defines osteopenia. The Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) estimates 10-year fracture probability and guides treatment decisions. Management begins with non-pharmacologic measures: adequate calcium (about 1000 to 1200 mg daily from diet and supplements if needed), vitamin D (800 IU daily in older adults), weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention, smoking cessation, and limiting alcohol. Pharmacologic treatment is indicated for a T-score of -2.5 or lower, a prior fragility fracture, or a high FRAX probability. First-line agents are bisphosphonates, most commonly oral alendronate once weekly, taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, remaining upright for 30 minutes to avoid oesophageal irritation; risedronate and intravenous zoledronic acid are alternatives. Denosumab, a RANKL inhibitor given subcutaneously every 6 months, is an effective alternative. Oestrogen therapy, raloxifene, teriparatide, and romosozumab are used in selected patients. Calcium and vitamin D must be adequate during therapy. Atypical femoral fractures and osteonecrosis of the jaw are rare complications of prolonged bisphosphonate use, which motivates the concept of a drug holiday after 3 to 5 years in lower-risk patients.

title: Osteoarthritis
content: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common joint disease, caused by progressive loss of articular cartilage with subchondral bone changes, osteophyte formation, and mild synovitis. It is strongly age-related and affects the knees, hips, hands (especially the first carpometacarpal joint and distal interphalangeal joints), and spine. Risk factors include older age, female sex, obesity, prior joint injury, repetitive joint loading, and family history. The cardinal symptom is joint pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest, with morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes; later features include crepitus, bony enlargement, reduced range of motion, and functional limitation. Inflammatory markers such as CRP are typically normal, and joint aspiration, if performed, shows non-inflammatory fluid. Radiographs may show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and cysts, but radiographic severity correlates poorly with symptoms. Management is multimodal. Core treatment includes education, weight loss, and exercise, both aerobic and strengthening, because quadriceps strengthening reduces knee pain; physiotherapy and activity modification help. Paracetamol may be used for mild pain, and topical NSAIDs are preferred for knee and hand OA because of fewer systemic effects. Oral NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen or naproxen, are effective but should be used at the lowest effective dose, with gastroprotection in at-risk patients and caution in renal disease and cardiovascular disease. Intra-articular corticosteroids provide short-term relief; hyaluronic acid injections are not routinely recommended. Opioids and duloxetine are options for refractory pain. Total joint replacement is highly effective for advanced symptomatic OA of the hip or knee after failure of conservative measures.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
content: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterised by symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, predominantly affecting the small joints of the hands and feet: the metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints, and wrists. Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 to 60 minutes is characteristic. Untreated, RA causes progressive joint erosions and deformity. Extra-articular manifestations include rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by positive rheumatoid factor or anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies and elevated inflammatory markers, with erosions or periarticular osteopenia on radiographs; anti-CCP is highly specific. The goal of treatment is remission or low disease activity, and the guiding principle is early, aggressive therapy, because joint damage accrues early. Methotrexate is the anchor drug, a folate antagonist given weekly at 15 to 25 mg with daily folic acid to reduce side effects such as mouth ulcers, hepatotoxicity, and bone marrow suppression. If the target is not reached within 3 to 6 months, a biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD is added: TNF inhibitors such as adalimumab and etanercept, or alternatives such as tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept, and the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib. Short courses of corticosteroids bridge the gap while DMARDs take effect, but long-term steroids are avoided. NSAIDs provide symptom relief only. Disease activity is monitored with composite scores such as DAS28, and joint damage with periodic radiographs. Methotrexate is teratogenic, so contraception is essential in women of childbearing age. Patients should receive influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, and live vaccines are avoided during immunosuppressive therapy.

title: Gout: Acute Attacks and Urate Lowering
content: Gout is the most common inflammatory arthritis in adults, caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues when serum urate is supersaturated. It classically presents as an acute, intensely painful, red, swollen joint, most often the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), with onset overnight and maximal pain within 24 hours; the knee, ankle, and midfoot are also common sites. Triggers include alcohol, purine-rich foods such as red meat and shellfish, dehydration, diuretics, and starting urate-lowering therapy. The diagnosis can be made clinically, but definitive confirmation is by joint aspiration showing negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light. Serum urate is often elevated but can be normal during an acute attack. Acute attacks are treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as naproxen or indomethacin, colchicine started early (within 12 to 36 hours), or corticosteroids for patients with contraindications; the earlier treatment starts, the more effective it is. Colchicine can cause diarrhoea, and the dose must be reduced in renal impairment. Urate-lowering therapy is indicated for recurrent attacks, tophi, or radiographic damage; the target serum urate is below 6 mg/dL (below 5 mg/dL with tophi). Allopurinol is the first-line urate-lowering agent, started at a low dose and titrated slowly; because starting therapy can precipitate attacks, prophylaxis with colchicine or an NSAID is given for the first 3 to 6 months. Febuxostat is an alternative for patients intolerant of allopurinol. Lifestyle measures include weight loss, limiting alcohol and sugary drinks, and avoiding thiazide and loop diuretics where possible. Chronic gouty tophi, nephrolithiasis, and erosive arthropathy are complications of poorly controlled disease.

title: Migraine: Diagnosis and Treatment
content: Migraine is a common primary headache disorder affecting about 15 percent of the population, with a female predominance. Attacks last 4 to 72 hours and are characterised by moderate to severe, often unilateral, throbbing headache aggravated by routine physical activity, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. About one third of patients experience aura, typically visual (scintillating scotoma, fortification spectra) but also sensory or speech disturbance, developing gradually over 5 to 60 minutes before the headache. Chronic migraine is defined as 15 or more headache days per month, at least 8 of them migrainous, for more than 3 months. Triggers include stress, menstruation, skipped meals, sleep disturbance, alcohol, and specific foods. Diagnosis is clinical; neuroimaging is not routinely needed unless red flags are present: thunderclap onset, fever and neck stiffness, new headache after age 50, progressive worsening, focal neurological deficit, or headache with immunosuppression or cancer. Acute treatment should be started early: simple analgesics such as ibuprofen 400 to 800 mg or paracetamol, with an antiemetic such as metoclopramide; triptans such as sumatriptan are first-line specific therapy for moderate to severe attacks and are contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, and previous stroke. Opioids and barbiturates should be avoided, and acute medication use limited to 2 to 3 days per week to prevent medication-overuse headache. Preventive therapy is offered when attacks are frequent or disabling: beta blockers such as propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, or candesartan are oral options; CGRP monoclonal antibodies such as erenumab and galcanezumab are newer preventive agents. Lifestyle regularisation, including regular sleep and meals, is foundational.

title: Epilepsy and Seizures
content: Epilepsy is a disease of the brain defined by an enduring predisposition to generate epileptic seizures, diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or one unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk. Seizures are classified as focal or generalised. Focal seizures arise in one hemisphere; awareness may be impaired (complex partial) or preserved, and they may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. Generalised seizures involve both hemispheres from onset and include absence seizures (brief staring spells), myoclonic jerks, and generalised tonic-clonic seizures. A first seizure is investigated with an ECG, blood tests including glucose and electrolytes, and an EEG; MRI brain is recommended to look for structural causes such as tumours, cortical dysplasia, or mesial temporal sclerosis. Provoked seizures, due to hypoglycaemia, alcohol withdrawal, hyponatraemia, or drug toxicity, are not epilepsy. Management is with antiseizure medications chosen by seizure type: sodium valproate, lamotrigine, or levetiracetam for generalised seizures, and lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, or oxcarbazepine for focal seizures. Valproate is highly teratogenic and is avoided in women of childbearing potential where alternatives exist. Medication is started after a second seizure in most cases and titrated to the lowest effective dose; about two thirds of patients become seizure-free with the first or second agent. Status epilepticus, a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery, is a medical emergency treated with intravenous lorazepam or intramuscular midazolam, followed by phenytoin or levetiracetam. Driving restrictions apply in most jurisdictions after a seizure, and patients with ongoing seizures should be counselled on safety, including around water and heights. Women with epilepsy require pre-conception counselling because some drugs interact with oral contraceptives and increase fetal malformation risk.

title: Parkinson's Disease
content: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with accumulation of Lewy bodies. The classic motor features are the triad of bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor, often described as pill-rolling and asymmetric at onset; postural instability develops later. Bradykinesia is the essential feature for diagnosis. Non-motor features are common and often precede motor symptoms: anosmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, anxiety, and later cognitive impairment and dementia. Diagnosis is clinical; dopamine transporter (DaT) imaging and MRI help exclude mimics such as drug-induced parkinsonism, essential tremor, and atypical parkinsonian syndromes such as multiple system atrophy. There is no cure, and treatment is symptomatic. Levodopa, combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor such as carbidopa, remains the most effective treatment; it is started when symptoms impair function. Levodopa is usually taken three to four times daily, and long-term use is associated with motor fluctuations (wearing off) and dyskinesias. Dopamine agonists such as ropinirole and pramipexole are alternatives, especially in younger patients, but carry risks of impulse control disorders, somnolence, and oedema. MAO-B inhibitors such as rasagiline and selegiline provide mild benefit. Advanced disease with troublesome fluctuations may be treated with deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus, apomorphine injections, or levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel. Amantadine helps dyskinesias. Physiotherapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy are integral, and falls prevention becomes critical as postural instability progresses. Levodopa should never be stopped abruptly because of the risk of neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome.

title: Alzheimer's Disease and Dementia
content: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, accounting for about 60 to 70 percent of cases. It is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with extracellular amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. The earliest and most prominent feature is impaired short-term memory, with difficulty learning new information; as the disease progresses, language, visuospatial function, executive function, and judgment decline, and behavioural changes such as apathy, agitation, and psychosis may appear. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by cognitive testing such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA); blood tests exclude reversible causes including hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, and syphilis. Structural imaging with CT or MRI excludes tumours, subdural haematoma, and normal pressure hydrocephalus; amyloid PET and CSF amyloid and tau biomarkers increase diagnostic confidence in atypical or early-onset cases. Vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, and frontotemporal dementia are important differentials. There is no disease-modifying cure, though amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibodies have recently been approved for early disease in selected patients. Symptomatic treatment uses acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, which provide modest cognitive benefit; memantine, an NMDA antagonist, is used in moderate to severe disease. Non-pharmacologic management is central: cognitive stimulation, structured routines, caregiver education and support, and safety measures such as driving assessment and home modification. Antipsychotics should be used sparingly for severe behavioural symptoms because of increased mortality and stroke risk in dementia. Advance care planning should begin early. The course is typically 8 to 10 years from diagnosis to death, and cardiovascular risk factor control may delay onset.

title: Major Depressive Disorder
content: Major depressive disorder is a common and disabling illness characterised by at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), accompanied by at least five symptoms from: sleep disturbance, appetite or weight change, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide. The PHQ-9 questionnaire is a useful screening and severity tool. Depression is underdiagnosed, and asking about suicidal ideation directly does not increase risk and can be life-saving. Mild depression can be managed with watchful waiting, exercise, sleep hygiene, and guided self-help; moderate to severe depression benefits from antidepressants, psychotherapy, or both. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as sertraline, fluoxetine, and escitalopram are first-line because of tolerability and safety; serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) such as venlafaxine and duloxetine are alternatives. Antidepressants take 2 to 4 weeks to begin working and up to 6 to 8 weeks for full effect; the dose should be titrated and the response reviewed at 2 to 4 weeks. Side effects include nausea, insomnia or sedation, sexual dysfunction, and a transient increase in anxiety; there is a small increased risk of suicidal thoughts in young people in the first weeks, so early review matters. Treatment is continued for at least 6 to 12 months after remission to prevent relapse, and stopped gradually to avoid discontinuation syndrome. Cognitive behavioural therapy and interpersonal therapy are effective, as are exercise and behavioural activation. Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression. Screening for bipolar disorder is important because antidepressants can trigger mania. Depression is common after stroke, myocardial infarction, and in chronic medical illness, and it worsens outcomes of these conditions.

title: Generalised Anxiety Disorder
content: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterised by excessive, uncontrollable worry about a range of everyday topics, present on more days than not for at least 6 months, accompanied by somatic symptoms such as muscle tension, restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and sleep disturbance. The worry is disproportionate to the actual circumstances and difficult to control. GAD frequently coexists with depression, and it is one of the most common anxiety disorders in primary care. Physical symptoms often drive patients to seek repeated medical investigations; palpitations, chest tightness, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms are common. Screening instruments include the GAD-7 questionnaire. First-line treatment is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) such as escitalopram or sertraline, or a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) such as venlafaxine or duloxetine; they take several weeks to act and may transiently worsen anxiety at initiation, so starting at a low dose is recommended. Pregabalin is an alternative with a faster onset. Benzodiazepines such as diazepam and lorazepam provide rapid short-term relief but are not recommended beyond 2 to 4 weeks because of tolerance, dependence, sedation, and falls risk, especially in older adults; if used, they are a bridge while the antidepressant takes effect. Psychological therapy, particularly cognitive behavioural therapy, is at least as effective as medication and is the preferred first step in mild to moderate GAD. Lifestyle measures include regular exercise, limiting caffeine and alcohol, and sleep hygiene. Beta blockers such as propranolol are useful for situational performance anxiety but not for GAD itself. Buspirone and hydroxyzine are weaker alternatives. Treatment response is reviewed at 4 to 6 weeks, and remission takes 6 to 12 months of continued treatment.

title: Insomnia: Assessment and Treatment
content: Insomnia is a disorder of initiating or maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening, despite adequate opportunity for sleep, causing daytime impairment, present at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months (chronic insomnia). Predisposing factors include genetic vulnerability and anxiety; precipitating factors include stress, illness, shift work, and medications such as corticosteroids and stimulants; perpetuating factors include poor sleep habits, excessive time in bed, and worry about sleep. Sleep hygiene is the foundation of non-pharmacologic care: regular sleep and wake times, a cool dark quiet bedroom, avoiding caffeine after midday, avoiding alcohol as a sleep aid, limiting screen time before bed, and avoiding long daytime naps. The treatment of choice for chronic insomnia is cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which combines stimulus control (going to bed only when sleepy, leaving the bed if awake), sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring, and relaxation; it is more durable than medication and is delivered in 4 to 8 sessions or via digital programmes. Pharmacotherapy is used short-term, ideally in combination with CBT-I: the Z-drugs zolpidem and zopiclone, and benzodiazepines, are effective but cause tolerance, dependence, rebound insomnia, and falls, particularly in the elderly, so they are limited to 2 to 4 weeks at the lowest effective dose. Melatonin has a modest effect, mainly in circadian disorders and older adults. Sedating antidepressants such as low-dose doxepin and trazodone are used off-label. Underlying causes should be treated: restless legs syndrome, obstructive sleep apnoea, chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. Insomnia in shift workers and jet lag responds to timed melatonin and strategic light exposure. Persisting insomnia increases the risk of depression, hypertension, and diabetes, so it merits active treatment rather than acceptance.

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea
content: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a disorder of repeated upper airway collapse during sleep, causing apnoeas and hypopnoeas, intermittent hypoxia, and sleep fragmentation. It is diagnosed when the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) is 5 or more events per hour with symptoms, or 15 or more events per hour regardless of symptoms; severity is graded mild (5-14), moderate (15-29), and severe (30 or more). Loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, and gasping are classic features; daytime sleepiness is the key daytime symptom, measured with the Epworth Sleepiness Scale. Risk factors are obesity (particularly central), male sex, older age, enlarged tonsils, retrognathia, and alcohol or sedatives before bed. OSA is associated with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and road traffic accidents from sleepiness. Diagnosis is confirmed by overnight polysomnography or home sleep apnoea testing. The first-line treatment for moderate to severe OSA is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), which splints the airway open; adherence is the main challenge, and side effects such as mask leak, claustrophobia, and nasal congestion can be managed with mask fitting, humidification, and pressure adjustment. Weight loss is highly effective: a 10 percent reduction in weight can reduce the AHI substantially, and bariatric surgery improves or resolves OSA in many patients. Positional therapy helps those with supine-only OSA. Mandibular advancement devices are an alternative for mild to moderate OSA, particularly in patients intolerant of CPAP. Tonsillectomy is curative in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy. Untreated severe OSA carries an increased risk of cardiovascular events; treatment with CPAP reduces sleepiness and blood pressure.

title: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
content: Atopic dermatitis, commonly called eczema, is a chronic inflammatory, pruritic skin condition with a relapsing course, often beginning in infancy. It results from epidermal barrier dysfunction and type 2 immune dysregulation, and it is strongly associated with the atopic march: food allergy, asthma, and allergic rhinitis. Lesions are erythematous, scaly, and intensely itchy patches; in infants they affect the face and extensor surfaces, while in older children and adults the flexures (elbow creases, behind the knees) are typical. Scratching leads to lichenification, excoriations, and secondary bacterial infection, most commonly with Staphylococcus aureus. The diagnosis is clinical. Management is stepwise. Emollients are the cornerstone of maintenance: thick, fragrance-free moisturisers applied liberally and frequently, including after bathing, repair the skin barrier and reduce flares. Trigger avoidance includes irritants such as soaps and wool, and identified allergens. Mild flares are treated with topical corticosteroids of appropriate potency, such as hydrocortisone 1 percent for the face and moderate potency agents such as betamethasone for the body, used in short courses; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are steroid-sparing options for sensitive areas. Moderate to severe disease may need phototherapy, systemic immunosuppressants such as ciclosporin or methotrexate, and the newer biologic dupilumab, an anti-IL-4/IL-13 antibody, which is highly effective. Wet wrap therapy helps acute severe flares. Itch is treated with emollients, topical steroids, and sedating antihistamines at night; the role of regular antihistamines is limited. Education about the chronic relapsing nature, bathing technique, and the steroid phobia is essential for adherence.
