title: Psoriasis
content: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease affecting about 2 to 3 percent of the population. The most common form, plaque psoriasis, presents with well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered by silvery scales on the extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, and lower back. The Koebner phenomenon describes lesions appearing at sites of trauma. Nail involvement causes pitting and onycholysis, and scalp psoriasis is very common. Psoriasis is associated with psoriatic arthritis in up to 30 percent of patients, presenting with inflammatory joint pain, dactylitis (sausage digit), enthesitis, and nail disease; it is also associated with cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes, and depression. Diagnosis is usually clinical; skin biopsy helps in atypical cases. Treatment is stratified by severity and joint involvement. Mild localised disease is treated with topical agents: potent corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues such as calcipotriol, or combination products; tar and dithranol are older options. Emollients help all patients. Phototherapy with narrowband UVB is effective for moderate disease. Moderate to severe plaque psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis requires systemic therapy: methotrexate, ciclosporin, or acitretin are traditional agents, and biologic therapies targeting TNF, IL-17, IL-23, or IL-12/23, such as adalimumab, secukinumab, and ustekinumab, achieve high clearance rates and are increasingly first-line for severe disease. Screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B is required before biologic therapy. Comorbidities should be actively screened: blood pressure, lipids, glucose, and joint symptoms at review. Psoriasis fluctuates, and triggers such as stress, infection, and some drugs (lithium, beta blockers, antimalarials) can provoke flares.

title: Cataracts
content: A cataract is opacification of the crystalline lens of the eye, the leading cause of reversible blindness worldwide. Age is the dominant risk factor; other causes include diabetes, prolonged corticosteroid use, smoking, ultraviolet light exposure, trauma, and congenital or genetic syndromes. Symptoms develop gradually: painless, progressive blurring of vision, glare and haloes around lights, difficulty with night driving, fading of colours, and frequent changes in spectacle prescription. A myopic shift can occur as the lens swells. Diagnosis is made by slit-lamp examination showing lens opacification. Early cataracts are managed conservatively with updated spectacles, brighter lighting, and anti-glare lenses; there are no effective medical treatments, although antioxidant intake and smoking cessation may slow progression. Surgery is the only definitive treatment and is one of the most common and successful operations worldwide. Phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation is the standard technique: the opacified lens is fragmented with ultrasound through a small corneal incision, removed, and replaced with a foldable artificial lens, usually under local anaesthesia as a day case. Surgery is indicated when visual symptoms impair daily activities such as driving, reading, or working, not based on a specific visual acuity threshold. Preoperative assessment includes biometry to choose the lens power; patients choosing monofocal lenses typically have excellent distance vision but still need reading glasses, while multifocal and toric lenses address presbyopia and astigmatism respectively. Complications are uncommon but include posterior capsule opacification (treated with YAG laser capsulotomy), infection (endophthalmitis), retinal detachment, and cystoid macular oedema. Patients should be warned to seek urgent review for pain, redness, or sudden vision loss after surgery.

title: Glaucoma: The Silent Thief of Sight
content: Glaucoma is a group of optic neuropathies characterised by progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells and characteristic optic disc cupping, the second leading cause of blindness worldwide. The major modifiable risk factor is raised intraocular pressure (IOP), though glaucoma can occur with normal pressure. Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the most common form: the drainage angle is open but aqueous outflow is impaired, and it is asymptomatic until advanced, with gradual loss of peripheral (peripheral visual field) vision, hence the name silent thief of sight. Angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency: the iris blocks the drainage angle, causing a rapid rise in IOP with severe eye pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, haloes around lights, and a red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil; it requires immediate treatment to prevent permanent vision loss. Diagnosis of POAG is by tonometry, optic disc examination (increased cup-to-disc ratio, disc haemorrhages), and automated perimetry showing glaucomatous visual field defects; OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer detects early damage. Treatment lowers IOP to slow progression. First-line therapy is a topical prostaglandin analogue such as latanoprost, given once daily at night, which increases uveoscleral outflow; side effects include conjunctival hyperaemia, eyelash growth, and iris darkening. Beta blockers such as timolol, alpha agonists such as brimonidine, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dorzolamide are alternatives or additions. Laser trabeculoplasty is an option for open-angle glaucoma, and surgery, most commonly trabeculectomy or tube drainage, is used when medical therapy fails or is poorly tolerated. Screening is important: adults over 40, especially those with a family history, diabetes, or African ancestry, should have regular eye examinations. Vision lost to glaucoma cannot be restored, so lifelong adherence to treatment is critical.

title: Age-Related Macular Degeneration
content: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a progressive disease of the macula, the central part of the retina responsible for sharp central vision, and the leading cause of irreversible blindness in older adults in developed countries. There are two forms. Dry (non-neovascular) AMD, accounting for 85 to 90 percent of cases, is characterised by drusen (yellow deposits under the retina) and gradual atrophy of retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors, causing slowly progressive central vision loss. Wet (neovascular) AMD occurs when abnormal blood vessels grow beneath the retina and leak fluid or blood, causing sudden distortion (metamorphopsia) and rapid central vision loss. Early AMD is asymptomatic; patients may notice needing brighter light for reading and mild blur. The Amsler grid is a home screening tool: new distortion or missing areas should prompt urgent review. Risk factors are age, smoking (the strongest modifiable risk factor), family history, hypertension, and light eye colour. Diagnosis is by dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography (OCT), with fluorescein angiography in suspected wet AMD. There is no cure for dry AMD; management is the AREDS2 supplement (vitamins C and E, zinc, lutein, zeaxanthin) for intermediate disease, which slows progression modestly, plus smoking cessation and cardiovascular risk control. Wet AMD is treated urgently with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections, such as ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab, given every 4 to 12 weeks; early treatment can stabilise and sometimes improve vision. Photodynamic therapy is rarely used now. Low-vision rehabilitation, magnifiers, and occupational therapy help patients maintain independence. Patients with sudden painless loss of central vision should be seen by an ophthalmologist within days.

title: Dengue Fever
content: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. There are four serotypes, and infection with one serotype confers lifelong immunity to that serotype but only transient protection against others; subsequent infection with a different serotype carries a higher risk of severe dengue. After an incubation of 4 to 10 days, classic dengue fever presents with sudden high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia and arthralgia (breakbone fever), nausea, and a maculopapular rash. The illness has three phases: febrile, critical, and recovery. The critical phase begins around days 3 to 7, when fever falls and plasma leakage may occur, manifesting as haemoconcentration, ascites, pleural effusion, and thrombocytopenia; warning signs of severe dengue include persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, and a rapid drop in platelet count with rising haematocrit. Severe dengue (dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome) can be fatal without careful fluid management. Diagnosis is by NS1 antigen or PCR in the first 5 days, and IgM serology thereafter. There is no specific antiviral; management is supportive, and the cornerstone is meticulous fluid balance: oral rehydration for most, and judicious intravenous fluids in the critical phase, titrated to haematocrit and urine output. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin are avoided because of bleeding risk; paracetamol is used for fever. Platelet transfusions are not given for a low platelet count alone. Most patients recover fully, but the critical phase requires close monitoring, ideally daily full blood counts until the fever has resolved and platelet counts are rising. Vector control, including removal of standing water and use of repellents, is the main preventive strategy; a live attenuated dengue vaccine is available in some countries for previously infected individuals.

title: Malaria
content: Malaria is a life-threatening parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium species, transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe disease and is responsible for nearly all deaths; P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae cause milder illness, though P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) that cause relapses. The classic paroxysm is fever, rigors, and sweating occurring cyclically, with headache, myalgia, nausea, and vomiting; the fever pattern (tertian or quartan) reflects the parasite's erythrocytic cycle. Symptoms usually begin 10 days to 4 weeks after exposure but can be delayed by months. Falciparum malaria can progress rapidly to severe disease: cerebral malaria with impaired consciousness and seizures, severe anaemia, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema, hypoglycaemia, acidosis, and multi-organ failure. Anyone with fever returning from an endemic area must be tested for malaria urgently. Diagnosis is by thick and thin blood films, or rapid diagnostic tests detecting parasite antigens; PCR is used in specialised settings. Treatment depends on species and severity. Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), such as artemether-lumefantrine, for 3 days. Severe malaria is a medical emergency treated with intravenous artesunate, followed by a full oral ACT course. P. vivax and P. ovale are treated with an ACT or chloroquine where sensitive, plus a course of primaquine to eradicate hypnozoites and prevent relapse; G6PD deficiency must be checked before primaquine because it can cause haemolysis. Chemoprophylaxis for travellers includes atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, or mefloquine, plus mosquito avoidance with repellents, long sleeves, and insecticide-treated bed nets. Pregnant women and children are at highest risk of severe disease.

title: COVID-19: Clinical Features and Management
content: COVID-19 is the disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, transmitted by respiratory droplets and aerosols. The incubation period is 2 to 14 days, typically 4 to 5. Most infections are mild or asymptomatic, with common symptoms of fever, cough, sore throat, myalgia, fatigue, anosmia or ageusia, and headache. A minority progress to pneumonia with dyspnoea and hypoxaemia, and a small proportion develop acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), sepsis, thromboembolism, and multi-organ failure. Risk factors for severe disease include older age, chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, and immunocompromise. Diagnosis is by reverse transcription PCR or rapid antigen tests on respiratory samples. Management depends on severity. Mild illness is managed at home with rest, fluids, and paracetamol, with instructions on when to seek care: breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, or oxygen saturation below 94 percent. Moderate illness may benefit from antiviral therapy in at-risk outpatients, such as nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) started within 5 days of symptom onset. Hospitalised patients with hypoxia receive dexamethasone (which reduced mortality in the RECOVERY trial) and therapeutic anticoagulation, with remdesivir in selected patients and tocilizumab or baricitinib in those with hyperinflammation. Oxygen, non-invasive ventilation, and prone positioning are supportive mainstays. Prevention relies on vaccination, which markedly reduces severe disease and death; updated vaccines target circulating variants. Long COVID, a syndrome of persistent fatigue, brain fog, dyspnoea, and other symptoms lasting months after infection, is recognised and managed symptomatically with rehabilitation. Infection control, including hand hygiene, ventilation, and masking in healthcare settings, limits transmission.

title: Sepsis: Recognition and Management
content: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is sepsis with circulatory and cellular metabolic abnormalities profound enough to increase mortality, defined by the need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg or more and a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Early recognition saves lives. Screening tools such as qSOFA (quick SOFA) use altered mental status, respiratory rate of 22 or more, and systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg or less; two or more criteria should prompt assessment for organ dysfunction. The Sepsis-3 definition requires an increase of 2 or more points in the SOFA score, indicating organ dysfunction. Common sources are pneumonia, urinary tract infection, abdominal infection, and skin and soft tissue infection. Management follows the hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour, start 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate of 4 mmol/L or more, and apply vasopressors for refractory hypotension. Source control, such as drainage of abscesses or removal of infected devices, is essential. Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor; hydrocortisone is added in refractory septic shock. In adults, the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends restrictive rather than liberal fluid strategy after the initial resuscitation. Target mean arterial pressure is 65 mmHg; lactate clearance and urine output guide adequacy of resuscitation. Blood glucose should be controlled, but early goal-directed therapy with ScvO2 targets is no longer recommended. Outcomes have improved with protocolised early recognition, but sepsis still carries high mortality, and survivors frequently suffer long-term cognitive, physical, and psychological sequelae requiring rehabilitation.

title: Meningitis and Encephalitis
content: Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, usually infectious. Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the leading causes in adults, and group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes in neonates and older adults. The classic triad is fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status, but patients may present with only headache and fever; photophobia, vomiting, and a petechial or purpuric rash (especially in meningococcal disease) are important clues. The rash in meningococcaemia does not blanch under a glass. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are less sensitive than commonly taught. Viral meningitis, usually enteroviral, presents similarly but is generally milder. Diagnosis requires lumbar puncture: bacterial meningitis shows a neutrophilic pleocytosis, raised protein, and low glucose; viral meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose; PCR identifies pathogens. Empirical antibiotics must not be delayed for imaging: if there are no contraindications, treatment starts immediately with a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, with ampicillin added for listeria coverage in older adults; dexamethasone given with or just before antibiotics reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis. Household contacts of meningococcal disease require antibiotic prophylaxis with rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone, and vaccination is part of prevention. Encephalitis, inflammation of the brain parenchyma, presents with fever, headache, altered behaviour, seizures, or focal deficits; herpes simplex encephalitis, which preferentially affects the temporal lobes, is treated with intravenous aciclovir, and delayed treatment is associated with high mortality and morbidity. HIV testing should be offered to all patients with meningitis.

title: Acute Appendicitis
content: Acute appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix and the most common surgical emergency of the abdomen. It most often affects adolescents and young adults, but it can occur at any age. The classic presentation is visceral periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant over 12 to 24 hours as parietal inflammation develops, accompanied by anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. McBurney's point tenderness, located one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, is the classic finding; guarding, rebound tenderness, and rigidity indicate peritoneal irritation. Atypical presentations are common in children, pregnant women (where the appendix is displaced by the gravid uterus), and the elderly, in whom pain may be minimal and perforation more likely. The Alvarado score and appendicitis inflammatory response (AIR) score help stratify risk. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by blood tests showing neutrophilia and a raised CRP, and imaging: ultrasound is first-line in children and pregnancy, while CT with intravenous contrast is highly sensitive and specific in adults. Differential diagnoses include mesenteric adenitis, gastroenteritis, ureteric colic, ovarian pathology, ectopic pregnancy, and Crohn's disease. Management is appendicectomy, increasingly performed laparoscopically, and intravenous antibiotics covering gram-negative and anaerobic organisms are given perioperatively. Uncomplicated appendicitis in selected patients may be treated with antibiotics alone, avoiding surgery in about two thirds of cases, though recurrence within a year is not uncommon. A periappendiceal abscess is treated with antibiotics and image-guided drainage, with interval appendicectomy later. Complications include perforation, peritonitis, and postoperative wound infection. Prompt recognition and surgery are associated with excellent outcomes.

title: Gallstones and Biliary Colic
content: Gallstones (cholelithiasis) are crystalline deposits in the gallbladder, classically described by the mnemonic for risk factors: female, fat, forty, fertile. Cholesterol stones predominate in Western populations; pigment stones are associated with haemolysis and cirrhosis. Most gallstones are asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging. Biliary colic occurs when a stone transiently obstructs the cystic duct: a constant, severe pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, often radiating to the back or right shoulder, typically starting 1 to 2 hours after a fatty meal, lasting 30 minutes to several hours, and resolving spontaneously. Nausea and vomiting may accompany the pain, but fever, jaundice, and persistent pain suggest complications. Acute cholecystitis, inflammation of the gallbladder, presents with prolonged pain, fever, and a positive Murphy sign (arrest of inspiration on deep palpation of the right upper quadrant), with raised inflammatory markers and a thickened gallbladder wall with pericholecystic fluid on ultrasound. Choledocholithiasis, a stone in the common bile duct, causes jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and deranged liver enzymes, and can lead to ascending cholangitis, a life-threatening emergency with Charcot's triad of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, to which shock and confusion add to form Reynolds' pentad. Symptomatic gallstones are treated with laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within days of presentation for acute cholecystitis; asymptomatic gallstones do not require surgery. Cholangitis requires urgent biliary drainage by ERCP plus antibiotics. Ursodeoxycholic acid dissolves small cholesterol stones slowly and has a high recurrence rate, so it is reserved for patients unfit for surgery. A low-fat diet reduces symptoms but does not dissolve stones.

title: Kidney Stones (Nephrolithiasis)
content: Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) are crystalline deposits that form in the urinary tract, affecting about 10 percent of people during their lifetime, with a male predominance and high recurrence. Calcium oxalate stones are the most common (about 70 to 80 percent); other types include calcium phosphate, uric acid, struvite (infection-related), and cystine stones. Risk factors include low fluid intake, a family history, hypercalciuria, hyperuricosuria, gout, diabetes, obesity, and certain medications. A stone passing into the ureter causes renal colic: severe, wave-like flank pain radiating to the groin, associated with nausea, vomiting, and haematuria; pain is often described as the worst pain experienced. Diagnosis is with non-contrast CT, the most sensitive imaging, or ultrasound in pregnancy; urinalysis shows haematuria, and infection should be excluded. Most stones smaller than 5 mm pass spontaneously with analgesia, hydration, and alpha blockers such as tamsulosin, which relax the ureter and increase passage rates; stones of 5 to 10 mm pass less often and may require intervention; stones larger than 10 mm rarely pass. Interventions include extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) for large renal stones. Urgent drainage by stenting or nephrostomy is needed for an obstructed infected kidney, anuria, or intractable pain. Uric acid stones, which are radiolucent, can be dissolved with alkalinisation of the urine using potassium citrate. Metabolic evaluation with 24-hour urine collection is offered to patients with recurrent stones. Preventive advice for calcium oxalate stones is high fluid intake to maintain urine output above 2 litres daily, moderate dietary calcium (not restriction), reduced sodium and animal protein, and limited oxalate-rich foods. Struvite stones require complete removal and treatment of the underlying infection.

title: Acute Pancreatitis
content: Acute pancreatitis is acute inflammation of the pancreas with autodigestion of the gland by prematurely activated pancreatic enzymes. Gallstones and alcohol account for about 70 to 80 percent of cases; other causes include hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, drugs, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, trauma, and autoimmune pancreatitis, with a small proportion idiopathic. The cardinal symptom is severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back, constant, and eased by leaning forward, with nausea and vomiting. The diagnosis requires two of three criteria: characteristic abdominal pain, serum amylase or lipase at least three times the upper limit of normal (lipase is more specific), and imaging findings of pancreatitis. Severity is assessed with scores such as the Glasgow-Imrie score or Ranson criteria, and by the presence of persistent organ failure, which defines severe pancreatitis; pancreatic necrosis, pseudocysts, and infected necrosis are local complications. Management is supportive: aggressive but balanced intravenous fluids, early oral or enteral feeding (within 24 to 48 hours) when tolerated, and analgesia; nasogastric decompression is not routine. Antibiotics are reserved for confirmed infection, not given prophylactically. In gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent obstruction, urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy is indicated; otherwise, cholecystectomy is performed during the index admission or within 2 weeks after mild gallstone pancreatitis to prevent recurrence. Severe pancreatitis is managed in intensive care, with enteral nutrition, and infected necrosis may require percutaneous or endoscopic drainage, or surgical necrosectomy. Prognosis is good for mild interstitial pancreatitis, with recovery in days; mortality is around 20 to 30 percent in severe necrotising disease. Alcohol cessation is mandatory in alcohol-induced disease.

title: Amoxicillin: A Broad-Spectrum Penicillin
content: Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin, a broad-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotic active against many gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Haemophilus influenzae, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. It is used for otitis media, sinusitis, community-acquired pneumonia, streptococcal pharyngitis, urinary tract infections in pregnancy, and as part of Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens. It works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis and is bactericidal. Amoxicillin is acid-stable and well absorbed orally, with a half-life of about 1 hour; it is excreted renally, so doses are reduced in significant renal impairment. It is usually given three times daily (or twice daily for some indications), with food to reduce gastrointestinal upset. Common side effects are diarrhoea, nausea, and rash; the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection is a concern with any broad-spectrum antibiotic. A non-allergic maculopapular rash is common with amoxicillin, particularly in patients with Epstein-Barr virus infection, and is distinct from true penicillin allergy, which manifests with urticaria, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. Patients with confirmed anaphylactic penicillin allergy should avoid amoxicillin and other beta-lactams; the cross-reactivity with cephalosporins is low but real. Amoxicillin-clavulanate (co-amoxiclav) adds clavulanic acid, a beta-lactamase inhibitor, extending cover to beta-lactamase-producing organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes, at the cost of more diarrhoea and a small risk of cholestatic jaundice. Amoxicillin is one of the most prescribed antibiotics worldwide, and stewardship principles, including using the shortest effective course, are important to limit resistance.

title: NSAIDs and Ibuprofen
content: Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis; this provides analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects but also causes the class's main toxicities. It is available over the counter for mild to moderate pain, fever, headache, dysmenorrhoea, and musculoskeletal pain, typically at 200 to 400 mg every 6 to 8 hours, with a maximum of 1200 mg daily without supervision and up to 3200 mg daily prescribed. It should be taken with food to reduce gastrointestinal irritation. The major adverse effects are gastrointestinal: dyspepsia, gastric erosions, and peptic ulcers with bleeding or perforation; the risk is higher with older age, high doses, concomitant aspirin, corticosteroids, or anticoagulants, and a history of peptic ulcer disease. Proton pump inhibitors provide gastroprotection in high-risk patients. Renal effects include reduced renal blood flow with acute kidney injury in hypovolaemic, elderly, or chronic kidney disease patients, and fluid retention. Cardiovascular risk is dose- and duration-dependent; high-dose NSAIDs increase the risk of myocardial infarction, heart failure, and stroke, and they are avoided in significant ischaemic heart disease. Ibuprofen can antagonise the antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin when taken together; taking ibuprofen at least 2 hours after aspirin or using another analgesic mitigates this. NSAIDs can precipitate bronchospasm in a minority of aspirin-sensitive asthmatics and are avoided in pregnancy after 20 weeks because of the risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus. Naproxen, diclofenac, and selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs) such as celecoxib share the class effects, with coxibs causing less gastrointestinal harm but similar cardiovascular and renal risk. Topical NSAIDs deliver efficacy with fewer systemic effects for localised musculoskeletal pain.

title: Statins and Atorvastatin
content: Statins are HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, the cornerstone of lipid-lowering therapy and cardiovascular risk reduction. By inhibiting the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis, they lower LDL cholesterol by 30 to 50 percent depending on intensity, and also stabilise atherosclerotic plaques, reduce inflammation, and lower cardiovascular events and mortality in both primary and secondary prevention. Atorvastatin is one of the most widely used statins, available in doses of 10 to 80 mg daily; high-intensity therapy is atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg, used after myocardial infarction, stroke, and in high-risk patients to achieve LDL targets, often below 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) in secondary prevention, and below 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) in very high risk. Statins are taken once daily, usually in the evening, although atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have long half-lives and can be taken any time. The most common side effects are myalgia and mild transaminase elevation; serious adverse effects are rare and include rhabdomyolysis, particularly with high doses or interacting drugs such as macrolides, azole antifungals, ciclosporin, and gemfibrozil, which inhibit CYP3A4 or OATP1B1 transport. Statins are contraindicated in pregnancy and active liver disease. In patients with myalgia and a normal creatine kinase, a dose reduction, switch to a different statin such as pravastatin or rosuvastatin, or alternate-day dosing can maintain therapy; statin-associated muscle symptoms are often over-attributed, and most patients tolerate another statin. Ezetimibe, a cholesterol absorption inhibitor, is added when targets are not met, and PCSK9 inhibitors are used in familial hypercholesterolaemia and very high risk. Beyond lipids, statins modestly reduce the risk of venous thromboembolism and atrial fibrillation, and they should not be stopped during acute illness.

title: Type 1 Diabetes
content: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. It typically presents in children and young adults, often abruptly, with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue, and sometimes with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening emergency with high blood glucose, ketones in blood and urine, acidosis, dehydration, and a fruity breath odour. Unlike type 2 diabetes, type 1 is not primarily associated with obesity or insulin resistance, and oral glucose-lowering agents are ineffective. Insulin therapy is mandatory from diagnosis and is lifelong: a basal-bolus regimen with long-acting basal insulin plus rapid-acting insulin before meals is standard. Patients must count carbohydrates and adjust doses accordingly. Blood glucose targets are individualised, typically 80 to 130 mg/dL before meals and below 180 mg/dL after meals. Screening for other autoimmune diseases, especially thyroid disease and coeliac disease, is recommended because they cluster together. Annual screening for complications mirrors type 2 diabetes: retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. Hypoglycaemia is common and must be treated promptly; patients should always carry fast-acting carbohydrate and glucagon for emergencies. Technology such as continuous glucose monitors and insulin pumps improves glycaemic control and quality of life. Education, including sick-day rules with extra insulin and ketone testing, is essential.

title: Prediabetes and Prevention of Diabetes
content: Prediabetes is an intermediate state of abnormal glucose metabolism that carries a high risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes. It is defined by an HbA1c of 5.7 to 6.4 percent, a fasting plasma glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL (impaired fasting glucose), or a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test value of 140 to 199 mg/dL (impaired glucose tolerance). Most people with prediabetes are asymptomatic, which is why opportunistic screening is recommended in adults with risk factors such as overweight, a family history of diabetes, hypertension, or a history of gestational diabetes. Prediabetes is not just a warning sign: it is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, and microvascular changes may already be present. The good news is that progression is not inevitable. The Diabetes Prevention Program trial showed that a lifestyle intervention achieving 7 percent weight loss with 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week reduced the incidence of diabetes by 58 percent over 3 years, and metformin reduced it by 31 percent. Lifestyle change is therefore the first-line intervention; metformin is considered for those at highest risk, particularly younger adults with obesity, women with prior gestational diabetes, or those with rising glucose despite lifestyle efforts. Follow-up includes repeat glucose testing at least annually, and monitoring of weight, blood pressure, and lipids. Some people revert to normal glucose regulation with successful weight loss. Statins are prescribed according to cardiovascular risk, not glucose status alone.

title: ACE Inhibitors: Class Effects and Side Effects
content: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, including lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, and perindopril, block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion. They lower blood pressure, reduce proteinuria, and slow the progression of chronic kidney disease, making them first-line in hypertension with diabetes or albuminuria, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and after myocardial infarction. Doses are titrated upwards; a dry cough occurs in 5 to 20 percent of patients and is the most common reason for discontinuation — it is caused by accumulation of bradykinin and usually resolves within days of stopping. Angioedema, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, is rare but potentially life-threatening and is an absolute contraindication to continuing the drug. A rise in serum creatinine of up to 30 percent after initiation is expected and acceptable; hyperkalaemia requires monitoring of electrolytes, especially in chronic kidney disease, in patients taking potassium-sparing diuretics or supplements, and in the elderly. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetotoxicity, particularly in the second and third trimesters, and in bilateral renal artery stenosis. Combined use with an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) is not recommended because it increases renal and hyperkalaemia risk without added benefit. If a patient cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor because of cough, switching to an ARB such as losartan is standard practice.

title: Beta Blockers: Uses and Precautions
content: Beta blockers antagonise beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate, contractility, and renin release. They are first-line in stable angina, after myocardial infarction, in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (where bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol succinate improve survival), and for rate control in atrial fibrillation. They are also used for migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, performance anxiety, and portal hypertension prophylaxis in cirrhosis. Propranolol, a non-selective agent, is used for tremor and migraine; cardioselective agents such as metoprolol and bisoprolol preferentially block beta-1 receptors. Common side effects include fatigue, cold extremities, bradycardia, and reduced exercise tolerance; sleep disturbance and vivid dreams occur, especially with lipophilic agents. Beta blockers can mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia, such as tremor and palpitations, in patients on insulin or sulfonylureas, and can worsen hypoglycaemia; sweating is usually preserved as a warning sign. They are relatively contraindicated in acute severe asthma because they can provoke bronchospasm — cardioselective agents are preferred when a beta blocker is essential in asthma or COPD, but they are not used in acute asthma. They should not be stopped abruptly after myocardial infarction because of rebound ischaemia; doses are tapered. Bradycardia, hypotension, and heart block are dose-limiting. In heart failure, beta blockers are started at low doses and up-titrated slowly, with close monitoring for fluid retention.

title: Calcium Channel Blockers
content: Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) relax vascular smooth muscle and reduce cardiac contractility and conduction by blocking L-type calcium channels. The dihydropyridines, amlodipine and nifedipine, act mainly on blood vessels and are widely used first-line for hypertension and stable angina; the non-dihydropyridines, verapamil and diltiazem, act on the heart and are used for rate control in atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardias, and angina. Amlodipine is a long-acting agent given once daily, starting at 5 mg, with excellent tolerability; the most common side effect is dose-dependent ankle oedema, which is not due to fluid retention and does not respond to diuretics. Flushing, headache, and palpitations can occur, especially at initiation. Dihydropyridine CCBs do not significantly depress cardiac conduction and can be combined safely with beta blockers for angina; verapamil and diltiazem, however, can cause bradycardia and heart block and should not be combined with beta blockers. Verapamil and diltiazem are avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction because of their negative inotropic effect, whereas amlodipine is safe in heart failure when needed for blood pressure control. CCBs are not contraindicated in asthma or diabetes, which makes them useful in patients with those conditions. Grapefruit juice increases levels of most CCBs and should be avoided, particularly with felodipine and nifedipine. Overdose causes severe hypotension and bradycardia and requires calcium, atropine, and inotropes.

title: Diuretics: Thiazides and Loop Diuretics
content: Diuretics increase urine output by reducing sodium reabsorption in the kidney. Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide and chlorthalidone, act on the distal convoluted tubule and are effective first-line antihypertensives; chlorthalidone is more potent and longer acting than hydrochlorothiazide. Loop diuretics, such as furosemide and bumetanide, act on the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and are the diuretics of choice in heart failure, pulmonary oedema, and chronic kidney disease, where their greater natriuretic ceiling matters. Loop diuretics are also used in cirrhosis with ascites. Thiazides are less effective when the glomerular filtration rate is below 30 mL/min, while loop diuretics retain efficacy. Adverse effects include hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia (which can precipitate gout), hyperglycaemia, and hypercalcaemia with thiazides; loop diuretics cause hypocalcaemia. Electrolytes and renal function should be checked 1 to 2 weeks after starting or up-titrating, then periodically. Furosemide is given once or twice daily; patients should take it early in the day to avoid nocturia. In heart failure, diuretic doses are titrated to euvolaemia, with daily weight monitoring at home, and over-diuresis causes pre-renal azotaemia and hypotension, especially with ACE inhibitors. Spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, is a potassium-sparing diuretic used in heart failure and resistant hypertension; it can cause painful gynaecomastia and hyperkalaemia, particularly with ACE inhibitors or in renal impairment.

title: Aspirin: Antiplatelet Use and Risks
content: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 in platelets, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis and platelet aggregation for the lifetime of the platelet, about 7 to 10 days. In the acute setting of myocardial infarction or ischaemic stroke, a 300 mg loading dose is chewed immediately to achieve rapid absorption; long-term secondary prevention uses low-dose aspirin, 75 to 100 mg daily. Aspirin is clearly beneficial in secondary prevention after myocardial infarction, stroke, or transient ischaemic attack, and after coronary stenting (combined with a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel as dual antiplatelet therapy). In primary prevention, the benefit is smaller and must be weighed against bleeding: low-dose aspirin is considered in selected adults aged 40 to 70 at high cardiovascular risk and low bleeding risk, and is generally not recommended in older adults because bleeding risk rises with age. The main adverse effect is gastrointestinal bleeding, which is reduced by a proton pump inhibitor in high-risk patients; aspirin can also cause allergic reactions, bronchospasm in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and rarely haemorrhagic stroke. Enteric-coated formulations do not clearly reduce bleeding. Aspirin should be stopped 5 to 7 days before elective surgery in most cases, but decisions around stents require cardiology input because of stent thrombosis risk. Ibuprofen taken before aspirin can block its antiplatelet effect, so ibuprofen should be taken at least 2 hours after aspirin when both are needed.

title: Hypertension in Pregnancy and Preeclampsia
content: Hypertensive disorders complicate about 5 to 10 percent of pregnancies. Chronic hypertension predates pregnancy or appears before 20 weeks; gestational hypertension arises after 20 weeks without proteinuria or organ dysfunction; preeclampsia is gestational hypertension plus proteinuria or evidence of end-organ involvement such as thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary oedema, or neurological symptoms. Preeclampsia is a major cause of maternal and fetal morbidity and presents with headache, visual disturbance, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, and oedema; seizures define eclampsia, which is treated with magnesium sulfate. Risk factors include first pregnancy, previous preeclampsia, family history, multiple pregnancy, obesity, chronic hypertension, renal disease, and autoimmune conditions. Low-dose aspirin (75 to 150 mg daily) from 12 weeks reduces the risk of preeclampsia in high-risk women. Diagnosis involves repeated blood pressure measurement and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, plus blood tests including platelets, creatinine, and transaminases, and fetal assessment with ultrasound and cardiotocography. Antihypertensive treatment is given for sustained severe hypertension (160/110 mmHg or higher) using labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and diuretics are avoided. Delivery is the definitive treatment, and timing balances maternal safety against fetal prematurity; severe preeclampsia at term is delivered promptly, while expectant management under close surveillance may be appropriate before 34 weeks. After delivery, blood pressure is monitored for several weeks because postpartum preeclampsia can occur.

title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
content: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is glucose intolerance first recognised in pregnancy, affecting about 6 to 9 percent of pregnancies. Screening is usually performed at 24 to 28 weeks with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test; GDM is diagnosed when fasting glucose is 92 mg/dL or higher, the 1-hour value is 180 mg/dL or higher, or the 2-hour value is 153 mg/dL or higher. Risk factors include overweight, family history of diabetes, previous GDM, previous large-for-gestational-age baby, and ethnicity with high diabetes prevalence. Untreated GDM increases the risk of macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, caesarean delivery, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and preeclampsia. Management begins with medical nutrition therapy and physical activity, with self-monitoring of blood glucose targets of fasting below 95 mg/dL and 1-hour postprandial below 140 mg/dL. When targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks, pharmacotherapy is added: insulin is the standard first-line treatment, and metformin is an alternative used in many centres. Women with GDM should be screened for diabetes 4 to 12 weeks postpartum with an oral glucose tolerance test, because up to half will develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years, and lifetime screening every 1 to 3 years is recommended. Breastfeeding is encouraged as it is associated with lower postpartum glucose levels. Babies of mothers with GDM should be monitored for hypoglycaemia after birth.

title: Anaemia of Chronic Disease
content: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD), also called anaemia of inflammation, is the second most common anaemia worldwide after iron deficiency, occurring in chronic infection, autoimmune disease, cancer, and chronic kidney disease. It results from hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration, reduced erythropoietin production and response, and shortened red cell survival: inflammatory cytokines, especially interleukin-6, stimulate hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages, making iron unavailable for erythropoiesis despite adequate total body stores. The anaemia is typically mild to moderate, normocytic or mildly microcytic, with a low serum iron and low transferrin but a normal or elevated ferritin, which is the key discriminator from iron deficiency, where ferritin is low. In patients with both ACD and iron deficiency, ferritin between 30 and 100 micrograms per litre with a transferrin saturation below 20 percent suggests coexisting deficiency. Treatment focuses on the underlying disease; erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are used in chronic kidney disease and some cancer-related anaemias, and intravenous iron is given when iron deficiency coexists, particularly in heart failure and inflammatory bowel disease. Red cell transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia or haemodynamic need. The anaemia of chronic kidney disease is driven by erythropoietin deficiency and responds to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents with iron supplementation; haemoglobin targets are typically 10 to 12 g/dL, avoiding overshoot, which increases thrombotic risk.

title: Sickle Cell Disease
content: Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene producing haemoglobin S, which polymerises under deoxygenation and deforms red cells into sickles that obstruct the microvasculature and haemolyse. It is most common in people of African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Indian ancestry. Chronic haemolysis causes anaemia, jaundice, gallstones, and an increased risk of infection because of functional asplenia. Acute vaso-occlusive crises cause severe bone pain, typically in the limbs, back, and chest, triggered by infection, dehydration, cold, hypoxia, or stress. Acute chest syndrome, a combination of chest pain, fever, hypoxia, and new infiltrates, is a leading cause of death. Other complications include stroke, priapism, avascular necrosis of the hip, leg ulcers, retinopathy, and chronic kidney disease. Newborn screening enables early diagnosis; prophylaxis with penicillin from infancy through childhood and vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, and meningococcus are essential because of the infection risk. Hydroxyurea raises fetal haemoglobin, reduces crisis frequency and mortality, and is offered to children and adults with recurrent crises. Acute crises are managed with rapid analgesia, fluids, oxygen if hypoxic, and treatment of precipitating infections; simple or exchange transfusion is used in acute chest syndrome, stroke, and priapism. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative for selected patients, and gene therapy has recently become available. Patients should avoid hypoxia during air travel, maintain hydration, and receive annual transcranial Doppler screening in childhood to stratify stroke risk.

title: Allergic Rhinitis
content: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by inhaled allergens such as pollen, house dust mites, animal dander, and moulds. Symptoms are sneezing, rhinorrhoea, nasal itching and congestion, and often itchy watery eyes, and they follow allergen exposure seasonally (hay fever) or perennially. It is associated with asthma, eczema, and conjunctivitis, and it impairs sleep, concentration, and school or work performance. Diagnosis is clinical; allergen skin prick testing or specific IgE can identify triggers when avoidance advice is needed. Management is stepped. Allergen avoidance and saline nasal irrigation help. Intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone and mometasone are the most effective treatment and are first-line for moderate to severe or persistent symptoms; they are safe for long-term use, with minor side effects of nasal dryness and occasional epistaxis. Oral antihistamines such as cetirizine and loratadine relieve sneezing and itching quickly and are useful for intermittent symptoms; first-generation sedating antihistamines such as chlorpheniramine and diphenhydramine should be avoided in the daytime because of sedation and impaired driving. Intranasal antihistamines such as azelastine and combination products are alternatives. Leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast are options in patients with coexisting asthma. Allergen immunotherapy, subcutaneous or sublingual, is disease-modifying and is offered for moderate to severe disease uncontrolled by medication or when avoidance is impossible; it reduces symptoms, medication use, and the risk of developing asthma in children. Decongestant nasal sprays should be limited to a few days because of rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa).

title: Anaphylaxis
content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction with rapid onset, involving the airway, breathing, or circulation, and usually skin or mucosal changes such as urticaria, flushing, or angioedema. Common triggers are foods (peanut, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, egg), insect venom (bee and wasp stings), and drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs, neuromuscular blockers). Symptoms include throat tightness, stridor, hoarseness, wheeze, dyspnoea, hypotension, collapse, abdominal pain, vomiting, and dizziness; cutaneous symptoms may be absent in up to 20 percent of reactions. Onset is usually within minutes of exposure, and biphasic reactions occur in up to 5 percent of patients hours later. Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first-line treatment and should be given immediately in the anterolateral thigh at a dose of 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) in adults, repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement; there is no contraindication in a life-threatening reaction. The patient is placed supine with legs elevated unless breathless. High-flow oxygen, intravenous fluids, and nebulised salbutamol are adjuncts; antihistamines and corticosteroids are second-line and do not treat airway obstruction or shock. All patients should be observed for 6 to 12 hours because of the biphasic risk and discharged with an adrenaline auto-injector, an anaphylaxis action plan, and referral to an allergy clinic to identify the trigger. Patients with venom allergy may benefit from venom immunotherapy. Penicillin allergy labels should be evaluated because they are frequently inaccurate and lead to suboptimal antibiotic choices.

title: Acute Otitis Media
content: Acute otitis media (AOM) is an acute infection of the middle ear, most common in children between 6 months and 2 years, frequently complicating a viral upper respiratory infection. The diagnosis requires acute onset of ear pain or fever plus otoscopic evidence of middle ear effusion with a bulging, erythematous, or perforated tympanic membrane. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis are the principal bacterial pathogens; viruses alone cause many cases. The natural history is favourable: most children improve without antibiotics within 2 to 3 days. The option of watchful waiting with analgesia is offered to children older than 6 months with mild to moderate symptoms, provided follow-up is assured; antibiotics are prescribed immediately for severe illness, children under 6 months, or those at higher risk. When antibiotics are used, high-dose amoxicillin (80 to 90 mg/kg/day) is first-line for 5 to 7 days; amoxicillin-clavulanate is used after recent amoxicillin exposure or when treatment fails after 48 to 72 hours. Paracetamol or ibuprofen relieves pain, which can be severe. Complications include perforation with otorrhoea, which usually heals spontaneously, acute mastoiditis with post-auricular swelling and pain requiring urgent ENT review, and rarely intracranial spread. Recurrent AOM, defined as three or more episodes in 6 months or four in a year, may be managed with tympanostomy tube insertion or a trial of prophylactic antibiotics in selected children. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccination has reduced the incidence of AOM substantially. Risk factors include daycare attendance, bottle feeding, parental smoking, and pacifier use.

title: Acute Rhinosinusitis
content: Acute rhinosinusitis is inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, usually viral, lasting up to 4 weeks. Symptoms include nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, facial pain or pressure over the maxillary or frontal sinuses, hyposmia, and headache worse on bending forward; fever may be present. Most cases resolve within 7 to 10 days without antibiotics, and antibiotics are the leading cause of inappropriate prescribing in upper respiratory illness. Bacterial superinfection, most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, should be suspected when symptoms persist beyond 10 days, worsen after initial improvement (double sickening), or are severe with fever above 39°C, purulent discharge, and facial pain for 3 to 4 days. Management is symptomatic: analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen, intranasal saline irrigation, intranasal corticosteroids in allergic patients, and decongestants for short-term relief; antihistamines are not helpful unless allergy coexists. When bacterial sinusitis is diagnosed, first-line treatment is amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5 to 7 days, with doxycycline as an alternative. Complications are rare but serious: periorbital cellulitis or abscess with eyelid swelling and pain on eye movement, meningitis, and intracranial abscess; orbital involvement requires urgent imaging and ENT/ophthalmology review. Recurrent acute sinusitis is defined as four or more episodes per year and may warrant CT imaging and evaluation for anatomic obstruction or allergic disease. Chronic rhinosinusitis lasts more than 12 weeks and is managed with nasal saline, intranasal corticosteroids, and sometimes surgery (functional endoscopic sinus surgery) for refractory polyposis or obstruction.

title: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
content: Herpes zoster, or shingles, results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus, which remains latent in dorsal root ganglia after chickenpox. It presents with a prodrome of burning, tingling, or shooting pain in a dermatomal distribution, followed within days by a unilateral vesicular rash that does not cross the midline. The rash crusts over in 7 to 10 days, and pain typically resolves within 2 to 4 weeks. The most common and feared complication is postherpetic neuralgia, defined as pain persisting more than 90 days after rash onset; its risk increases with age and is highest in those over 60. Other complications include bacterial superinfection, ophthalmic zoster (involving the first division of the trigeminal nerve, with a vesicle on the tip of the nose signalling nasociliary involvement) which can threaten vision and requires urgent ophthalmology review, Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy and ear vesicles, and, in immunocompromised patients, disseminated disease and visceral involvement. Antiviral therapy with aciclovir, valaciclovir, or famciclovir started within 72 hours of rash onset reduces acute pain, rash duration, and the risk of postherpetic neuralgia; it should be given regardless of timing in ophthalmic zoster, immunocompromise, or severe pain. Analgesia may require opioids or agents such as amitriptyline, gabapentin, or pregabalin. The recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is recommended for adults aged 50 and over and for immunocompromised adults, and it is highly effective at preventing zoster and postherpetic neuralgia. Shingles is contagious to people who have not had chickenpox via direct contact with vesicles, but not by airborne spread.

title: Cellulitis and Skin Infections
content: Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, entering through breaks in the skin such as cracks between toes, ulcers, insect bites, or wounds. It presents with an area of erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain, with poorly demarcated borders, often on the lower leg, and may be accompanied by fever and malaise. Bilateral leg redness, intense itching, or a clear-cut trauma story favour other diagnoses; venous eczema, stasis dermatitis, and deep vein thrombosis mimic cellulitis, so careful examination matters. Systemic features such as high fever, hypotension, or rapidly spreading erythema indicate severity and the need for intravenous antibiotics and consideration of necrotising fasciitis, an emergency with severe pain out of proportion, blistering, and skin discolouration, requiring urgent surgical debridement. Mild cellulitis is treated with oral antibiotics for 5 days: flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin, with clindamycin or doxycycline for penicillin allergy; if MRSA is suspected, doxycycline or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is added. Elevation of the limb and analgesia are important, and marking the erythema border helps monitor spread. Recurrent cellulitis of the lower leg is common; management includes treating tinea pedis, moisturising dry skin, and in frequent recurrences, prophylactic low-dose penicillin. Erysipelas is a superficial form with sharply demarcated, raised, bright red plaques. Patients with lymphoedema, diabetes, or peripheral arterial disease are at higher risk and need prompt treatment because of poorer outcomes.

title: Diverticulitis
content: Diverticulosis is the presence of outpouchings (diverticula) of the colonic wall, common in older adults, usually asymptomatic and found incidentally at colonoscopy. Diverticulitis occurs when diverticula become inflamed or infected, typically in the sigmoid colon, presenting with left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and change in bowel habit, often with nausea. Examination may reveal localised tenderness and guarding; a palpable mass suggests an abscess. The diagnosis is confirmed by CT with intravenous contrast, which also stages severity: uncomplicated diverticulitis shows colonic wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding, while complicated disease shows abscess, perforation with free air, fistula, or obstruction. Mild uncomplicated diverticulitis is often managed in the outpatient setting with a liquid diet, analgesia, and oral antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole, or amoxicillin-clavulanate, for 5 to 7 days; recent guidelines allow observation without antibiotics in selected immunocompetent patients with mild disease. Complicated diverticulitis requires hospitalisation, intravenous antibiotics, and often image-guided percutaneous drainage of abscesses larger than 3 to 4 cm, with elective sigmoid resection after resolution for recurrent attacks or after a complicated episode. Surgery (Hartmann's procedure or resection with anastomosis) is required emergently for free perforation with generalised peritonitis. Recurrent diverticulitis occurs in about a third of patients after a first episode; fibre-rich diet, adequate hydration, and avoidance of NSAIDs (which increase perforation risk) are advised. Bleeding from diverticula, usually painless and brisk, is managed with colonoscopy, and angiography or surgery if persistent.

title: Constipation in Adults
content: Constipation is defined by Rome IV criteria as two or more of: straining, lumpy or hard stools, sensation of incomplete evacuation, sensation of anorectal obstruction, manual manoeuvres, or fewer than 3 defecations per week, present for at least 3 months with symptom onset at least 6 months earlier. It affects up to 20 percent of adults, is more common in women and older people, and is often multifactorial: inadequate fibre or fluid, immobility, medications (opioids, iron, calcium channel blockers, anticholinergics), pelvic floor dysfunction, and conditions such as hypothyroidism, diabetes, and Parkinson's disease. Red flags requiring investigation are new symptoms after age 50, rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, family history of colorectal cancer, and a palpable abdominal or rectal mass; colonoscopy is indicated in these situations. Management starts with lifestyle measures: adequate fluid, gradual increase in fibre to 25 to 30 g daily, exercise, and regular toileting routines after meals. When laxatives are needed, osmotic agents such as polyethylene glycol are effective and well tolerated; lactulose and magnesium salts are alternatives. Stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl are used short-term and for opioid-induced constipation, often combined with an osmotic agent. Fibre supplements such as psyllium help when fibre intake is low, but may worsen slow-transit constipation. Pelvic floor dysfunction is treated with biofeedback rather than laxatives. Prucalopride and linaclotide are second-line prescription options for chronic refractory constipation. Opioid-induced constipation is best managed with prevention: adequate fluids, stimulant laxatives, and, in refractory cases, peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists such as naloxegol.

title: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
content: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is non-malignant enlargement of the prostate, extremely common in men over 50, causing lower urinary tract symptoms by bladder outlet obstruction: weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, straining, terminal dribbling, incomplete emptying, frequency, nocturia, and urgency. Complications include acute urinary retention, recurrent urinary tract infection, bladder stones, and chronic kidney disease from high-pressure retention. The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) quantifies severity. Digital rectal examination, PSA, renal function, and urinalysis are standard baseline tests; uroflowmetry and post-void residual measurement help when symptoms are moderate to severe. Men with a raised PSA require evaluation for prostate cancer, and haematuria or a hard nodule warrants urology referral. Watchful waiting with lifestyle advice (reduced evening fluids, caffeine and alcohol avoidance, timed voiding) is appropriate for mild symptoms. Medical therapy: alpha blockers such as tamsulosin relax prostatic smooth muscle and improve the flow rate within days; 5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride and dutasteride shrink the prostate over 3 to 6 months and are used for prostates larger than about 30 to 40 g, with side effects of reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, and rarely depression; combination therapy is more effective than either alone. Antimuscarinics such as solifenacin can be added for storage symptoms, and tadalafil is an alternative with benefit for coexisting erectile dysfunction. Surgery — transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), laser enucleation, or prostatectomy — is indicated for refractory symptoms, retention, or complications. Acute urinary retention is treated with catheterisation, and alpha blockers started at the time of catheter insertion improve the chance of successful trial without catheter.
